When you write important data to a Blu-ray Disc Recordable (BD-R), it's reasonable to wonder how long you can expect the disc to stay readable. According to the Canadian Conservation Institute (CCI), regular BD-R discs can last between 5 and 20 years. Proper storage is important for making them last, but factors at play also include the materials used to manufacture the BD-R; you need non-dye BD-R discs with a gold metal layer to achieve the 10- to 20-year part of that range. Interestingly, the CCI  found that rewritable BD-R (BD-RE) discs last even longer than standard BD-R, at 20 to 50 years. In any case, your optical disc storage habits are key to making sure your writable Blu-ray discs survive as long as the materials make possible. They need to be stored vertically in a dry, low-humidity place at temperatures between 14 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit. Never apply adhesive labels on the discs, and use only water-based permanent markers to label them. Of course, avoid scratching them, which means careful cleaning and the use of jewel cases instead of paper or plastic sleeves. Contrary to what you might expect, given that Blu-ray is a newer technology than DVDs, BD-R discs have a shorter lifespan than DVD-R. The same CCI study looking at the lifespan of various optical discs showed that DVD-R discs with a gold metal layer can last between 50 and 100 years with good storage habits. Of course, DVD-R discs can't hold nearly as much data as a BD-R can, but longer-lasting writable Blu-ray options do exist. Blu-ray discs built with M-Disc technology promise (in marketing, at least) a biblical-sounding 1,000 years of readable life. There's no research fully proving this claim, but a 2022 NIST study found that you can reasonably expect an M-Disc product to last for 100 years at minimum.  Another standard for BD-R discs, dubbed "DM for Archive" by Pioneer, claims 100 years of readable life. The standard was developed primarily to comply with a Japanese law on government archives, though, and unfortunately in the U.S., DM for Archive discs and drives are nearly impossible to find. Pioneer briefly sold a DM for archive-compliant and U.S. market-ready drive called the BDR-WX01DMU along with compliant discs, but they were discontinued in 2025. M-Disc drives and discs are much easier to find in the U.S., though they're pricier than standard BD-R. However, cutting-edge technology like Microsoft's Project Silica shows that you may have more extra-long-term storage options on the horizon.

Remote working from home has always been a thing, but post-COVID lockdowns showed employers that some workers are happier being away from the office. It requires solid communication to sync up with teams, and this raises the question: Is investing in a dedicated audio setup actually worth the money? The answer is absolutely, as relying on built-in microphones on a work-issued laptop is one of the biggest causes of ineffective meetings. So what's the best audio setup for work from home? Well, it starts with forgetting the laptop microphone and introducing a dedicated microphone into the daily workflow. And no one likes the sound of someone typing in a meeting, let's be honest. Upgrading to a standalone microphone makes sure that members of the team can focus on quality audio to better get messages across to colleagues. Plus, studies show that listeners often associate credibility and trustworthiness with better audio quality. A professional microphone setup is also a long-term investment, and there are even some clever uses for your PC's microphone outside of Zoom calls. Want to start a podcast or narrate video for a YouTube channel? It's all possible, even recording instruments and vocals for the musically talented. But knowing where to start with a solid microphone setup is the challenge, and we know a thing or two about USB streaming mics and XLR-powered broadcast condensers. There's an overwhelming amount of choice on the market, so what is the best microphone for work calls? That depends on a few factors, but we'll start with work environment. For those working in untreated rooms or a noisy household, a dynamic microphone with a cardioid pickup pattern is ideal as is cuts down on disruptive background noises. Next up is the connection type, which usually comes down to USB or XLR standard connections. USB microphones and headsets are great for plug-and-play functionality and work out of the box with most computers and software without extra hardware. However, with convenience, there are also few disadvantages of using USB microphones, such as lacking that broadcast-quality sound heard over the radio and on podcasts. For peak audio fidelity, an XLR microphone is the best bet, but it's going to require some extra hardware. To use an XLR microphone, we need an external audio interface or preamp to successfully connect it to a computer. There's some accessories, such as the Shure MVX2U, that skips the extra box on a desk and simply has an XLR input and a USB output. It packs a 60dB preamp, zero-latency monitoring, and 48V phantom power for that high-quality voice representation that's nice and discreet. Buying a microphone and necessary hardware is only half the battle; next up is using the right accessories and software for the best sound quality. Relying on a cheap desktop stand, for example, can transfer desk vibrations directly into the audio, so it's a good idea to mount a microphone to a dedicated boom arm.  This will provide some acoustic isolation while clearing up some desk space. It's the best of both worlds, plus the microphone can be repositioned closer to the user's mouth for the best pickup performance and be swung out of the way when not in use. Having any microphone suspended in a shock mount is going to dampen movement further, and a windscreen will cut out breathing and wind noise from the audio stream. XLR microphone audio quality can be significantly improved by plugging it into an external Thunderbolt or USB audio interface. For example, hardware like Apollo Solo is a great option as it gives users Unison preamps and UAD-2 SOLO processing over Thunderbolt 3. There are more modern audio improvement solutions available too, such as AI-powered noise reduction tools that can automatically filter out keyboard typing and air conditioning hum while keeping your voice clear.

What's the best year in movie history? That's a loaded question! Does it mean the year with the most good movies? The year with an outsized impact on the industry at large? The year when all the good movies succeeded at the box office and the bad ones flopped? Is it 1990 just because that's the year "Gremlins 2: The New Batch" was released? We explored this quandary when ranking the 14 greatest years in horror history, but now we're applying it to filmmaking writ large, the whole shebang. For me, it's a confluence of a little bit of everything, but mostly it's about years when a high number of foundational, critically acclaimed, or truly audience-pleasing films were released. We're talking years so dense with movies that were immediately revered or, with time, are now considered classics, leaving you either pining for the days when we had it so good or realizing you never actually knew how good we had it. Great movies come out every year, but these years felt like nothing but great movies. Here are the 15 best years in movie history, ranked. 1927 is one of the most important years in modern cinema: The industry broke the sound barrier, forcing Hollywood to overhaul its day-to-day operations. "The Jazz Singer" hit theaters in October with synchronized songs and a few snatches of spoken dialogue, and within a few years, the silent era was over. The art form reached a brief zenith in its proto-form before being completely reimagined, leaving dozens of former silent stars struggling to keep up with the modern age. Those movies from the last gasp of the silent era show the pure innovation in visual storytelling. Fritz Lang made "Metropolis," one of the most influential sci-fi movies of all time, whose DNA you can trace to the very essence of modern-day sci-fi we're so familiar with. Meanwhile, Murnau's "Sunrise" is a swooning, fluid love story that won an Oscar in the odd category of "Unique and Artistic Production." "Wings" took home the first-ever Best Picture trophy, and Abel Gance's "Napoléon" offered viewers a sprawling epic of ingenious technical skill. These movies hold up just as well against a century of talkies that followed. The movies of 1957 had a lot to say amid shifting cultural tides. Sidney Lumet made his feature debut with "12 Angry Men," a masterclass about sweaty jury room caught in an ethical quandary. But David Lean's sweeping WWII epic, "The Bridge on the River Kwai," was the one that took home seven Oscars, including Best Picture. Stanley Kubrick's "Paths of Glory" got no such love for its devastating portrait of military brass sending soldiers to die, but it remains one of the great war movies. Then there's the international circuit. Ingmar Bergman's "The Seventh Seal" cemented his status as one of cinema's most existential brooders, pondering the grave unknowability of life and death in lush visual fashion — and he doubled up by releasing "Wild Strawberries" the same year. Akira Kurosawa remade "Macbeth" in feudal Japan with "Throne of Blood." Federico Fellini's "Nights of Cabiria" won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, and I haven't even mentioned films like "Witness for the Prosecution" and "Sweet Smell of Success." The films of 1957 had a serious, sobering sensibility as they reckoned with the world around them, and they still resonate strongly. Many people consider 1939 the zenith of classic Hollywood. That's true, and the only reason it's so low is the sheer number of quality films the following years would offer. But the studio system was firing on every cylinder, with an absurdly great lineup of 10 Best Picture nominees at the Academy Awards. "Gone With the Wind" swept up eight competitive Oscars, including a historic win for Hattie McDaniel as the first Black performer to take home a statue. Victor Fleming got credit for it and "The Wizard of Oz," perhaps the ultimate cinematic classic for the ages. Elsewhere, "Mr. Smith Goes to Washington" gave us James Stewart's exhausted, hoarse-voiced filibuster, and John Ford's "Stagecoach" minted John Wayne as a Western movie star. Howard Hawks' "Only Angels Have Wings" gave Cary Grant and Jean Arthur career highlights, and Ernst Lubitsch's "Ninotchka" is secretly one of classic Hollywood's greatest romcoms. Right before a globe-shattering war, the Golden Age was in an endlessly rewarding victory lap. The blockbuster was born in 1975, and the era of New Hollywood brats was in full swing. Steven Spielberg's "Jaws" would forever change how the industry made and marketed spectacle-laden fare, and kick-start a franchise that ranges from garbage fire to masterpiece. "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest" swept the Big Five Oscars and featured one of Jack Nicholson's most iconic performances. Sidney Lumet makes his second appearance on this list with "Dog Day Afternoon," which features Al Pacino as a sweaty, desperate bank robber trying to raise money for his partner's gender-reassignment surgery. Elsewhere, things get more rarefied. Stanley Kubrick shot "Barry Lyndon" by pure candlelight with lenses originally developed for NASA, and the result is a movie that captures the essence of an epic, sprawling canvas hung in a museum. "Deep Red" is giallo at its most stylish, with Dario Argento's typically clever direction and a throbbing Goblin score. And Chantal Akerman's expansive 3-hour epic, "Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles," about a widow going through the quotidian motions, would go on to top Sight & Sound's poll of the greatest films ever made nearly 50 years later. While 1975 was New Hollywood at its apex, 1967 kicked the door open, challenging the industry and audiences with new, provocative, sometimes raucous films that broke the old studio-system mold. Just look at that year's Best Picture field, where "In the Heat of the Night" won, but the Academy also nominated "Doctor Dolittle," epitomizing the clash of titans as the tides turned. In any case, "Bonnie and Clyde" or "The Graduate" probably should have won instead, with their bare-faced, candid challenges to accepted societal mores in the '60s making them bastions of new ideas about what stories you could tell on screen. If you want more of everything this movement kicked off, you should check out our list of the best New Hollywood movies you probably haven't seen. Across the Atlantic, Catherine Deneuve lit up the movie screens, first in Luis Buñuel's "Belle de Jour," as a bored housewife living a secret double life, and then in Jacques Demy's candy colored "The Young Girls of Rochefort," where she twirls through a musical alongside her real-life sister, Françoise Dorléac. In 1967, cinema was rapidly developing new conventions. 1982 was the year of genre-movie masterpieces that contemporary audiences largely ignored. Steven Spielberg owned the summer with his generation-defining "E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial," while also producing "Poltergeist," Tobe Hooper's suburban shocker that people are convinced Speilberg ghost-directed. Meanwhile, "Blade Runner" and "The Thing" both crashed and burned at the box office, but both are now among the most influential sci-fi movies ever made — turns out plenty of genre-defining sci-fi barely impacts the box office. That includes "Tron," a landmark in computer imagery that kickstarted a franchise audiences across generations generally refuse to see in theaters. 1982 also introduced audiences to John Rambo in "First Blood," a movie about a haunted, wounded Vietnam Vet that became a franchise about Sylvester Stallone looking cool while shooting a gun. Martin Scorsese's "The King of Comedy" underperformed and was savaged by critics, but his acolytes now know it as one of his secret masterpieces. Jim Henson's beautiful puppet work made "The Dark Crystal" a defining Gen-X movie, Dario Argento kept delivering slick, bloody giallo with "Tenebre," and Ingmar Bergman released yet another three-hour domestic epic with "Fanny and Alexander" (actually five hours if you catch the television version). The market for adult-oriented Hollywood fare was never better than in the mid-'90s. Just look at "Heat," Michael Mann's crime epic that sets Robert De Niro and Al Pacino loose on an existential cat-and-mouse chase across L.A. David Fincher's gloriously nasty, grim "Se7en" took audiences on an apocalyptic journey of doom with Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman. "The Usual Suspects" spawned a thousand twist-ending imitators; Ron Howard made one of his best films with "Apollo 13"; and Martin Scorsese went on a gangster-movie victory lap with "Casino." Even the lighter popcorn and blockbuster fare was memorably stacked. This was the year Pierce Brosnan debuted as Bond in "GoldenEye," and also the year "Die Hard with a Vengeance" paired Bruce Willis with Samuel L. Jackson for the franchise's best sequel (as confirmed by our ranked list of the "Die Hard" franchise). You've also got "Crimson Tide," "Batman Forever," "Jumanji," and "Desperado," all with a certain level of impact, if you're from a certain generation of movie fans. Last but not least, you can't forget Amy Heckerling's farcical coming-of-age classic "Clueless," or "Toy Story," which redefined animation and launched a franchise. One little movie called "Star Wars" came out in 1977, which is probably justification enough for this year to be included. It's now 50 years later, and we're still feeling the ramifications of its cultural impact, both through the sustained "Star Wars" franchise universe of movies, games, merch, and more, and through its redefinition of what the cultural force of the blockbuster could look like. It's also part of why another 1977 masterpiece, William Friedkin's "Sorcerer," fell flat on its face but is now considered perhaps the last masterpiece of the declining New Hollywood era, despite its perfect storm of problems. 1977 horror also produced some weirdo masterpieces. Dario Argento adds another entry to this list with what many consider his opus, "Suspiria." David Lynch kickstarted his influential career of surrealist fever dreams with "Eraserhead," which began as a student production and became a regular-rotation midnight movie at repertory houses. Then there's Nobuhiko Obayashi's "House," a psychedelic Japanese haunted house movie where a man-eating piano is only the start of the truly batty imagery layered within. Dads of a certain age were eating well in 1987, a banner year for action and comedy flicks. Arnold Schwarzenegger kickstarted the still-ongoing sci-fi horror franchise with "Predator," which endures as one of the best movies of the '80s (and we've ranked the franchise if you want to see how the rest fares). Paul Verhoeven blasted audiences with a brutal, unforgiving satire of American policing and consumerism in "Robocop." Brian De Palma released his notable gangster movie before "Scarface" with "The Untouchables," and you also had "Full Metal Jacket," "Fatal Attraction," and "Wall Street." But comedies are where '87 really shines. "The Princess Bride" is an iconic, farcical fantasia for anyone who grew up with it, and the Coen brothers made an early masterpiece with the Looney Tunes energy of "Raising Arizona." Then you've got "Planes, Trains, and Automobiles," "Good Morning, Vietnam," "Spaceballs," "The Witches of Eastwick," and even "Beverly Hills Cop II," cementing a year that was good for making audiences laugh. 1974 is another high-water mark for the New Hollywood era, when filmmakers had total freedom and made grungy, bleak masterpieces that challenged the controlled order studios and producers had imposed on artistic visions. "The Godfather Part II" lived up to, and even surpassed, its predecessor's quality—and became one of only two sequels to win Best Picture. "Chinatown" presented an upsettingly nihilistic view of justice's viability in a legendary noir. You've also got another S-tier Francis Ford Coppola movie in "The Conversation," along with "A Woman Under the Influence," "Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore," and the grimy, thrilling "The Taking of Pelham 123." Among this more serious fare, Tobe Hooper released one of the most visceral and upsetting horror movies ever made with "The Texas Chain Saw Massacre."  1974 also delivered elsewhere on the genre side of things: Mel Brooks released both "Blazing Saddles" and "Young Frankenstein," two of the decade's most iconic comedies. "Black Christmas" helped invent the modern slasher. Brian De Palma restaged "Phantom of the Opera" with a Faustian twist in "Phantom of the Paradise." Yes, '74 was a rich lineup of boundary-pushing filmmakers. Hollywood crowd-pleasing instincts collided with the boom of mid-'90s indie filmmaking in 1994, to spectacular results. Quentin Tarantino's "Pulp Fiction" won Cannes' Palme d'Or and redefined the cultural conversation around movies for a young generation of movie fans. It lost Best Picture to "Forrest Gump," a colossal hit that remains a cultural lightning rod. It's also the year "The Shawshank Redemption" was born, and it has sat at the top of the IMDb Top 250 for decades. Disney's "The Lion King" became one of the biggest animated hits ever, and "Speed" is a tight and iconic Keanu Reeves action classic. In the mid-budget and comedy range, you had the continued airport-novel-adaptation boom with "The Client" and "Clear and Present Danger." Jim Carrey pretty much owned the box office with "Ace Ventura: Pet Detective," "The Mask," and "Dumb & Dumber." You even had family staples that would end up on constant rotation in households, like "The Santa Clause" and "The Little Rascals." 1994 had something for everyone, which is what helps it stand out across a century of moviemaking. The modern blockbuster tentpole took shape in 2001, backed by real craft. Fantasy, in particular, was having a banner year, with "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" and "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" each launching franchises that would define a generation of moviegoers. Animation was thriving too: "Shrek" became the first winner of the Best Animated Feature Oscar. It was also the year of Pixar's "Monsters, Inc.," and Hayao Miyazaki's "Spirited Away" is now championed as a breathtaking masterwork. And of course, "The Fast and the Furious," kickstarted a global franchise empire. But 2001 had plenty of weird stuff, too. David Lynch's "Mulholland Drive" began as a canceled TV pilot and now sits near the top of many critics' lists of the best 21st-century films. "Donnie Darko" went through its rite of passage, flopping at the box office before becoming a midnight-movie staple in rep houses and living rooms. Steven Spielberg finished Stanley Kubrick's unrealized sci-fi tragedy "A.I.: Artificial Intelligence," one of his most underrated works and a high-ranking entry on our list of Spielberg's sci-fi movies. Plus, you've got "The Others," "The Royal Tenenbaums," "Ocean's Eleven," and "Legally Blonde." 1971 was a fearless year for the New Hollywood auteurs, as filmmakers' bold visions came to life, and they got away with just about anything. That's how you have a year when Stanley Kubrick could release something as unsettlingly provocative as "A Clockwork Orange," or William Friedkin in a similar fashion with "The French Connection." There's also softer, more emotionally revealing titles, including Robert Altman's "McCabe & Mrs. Miller," Peter Bogdanovich's "The Last Picture Show," and Hal Ashby's oddball outsider romance "Harold and Maude." Plus, Steven Spielberg and George Lucas made their directorial debuts with "Duel" and "THX 1138," respectively. But the gritty fare stood out. Clint Eastwood earned a new iconic role in "Dirty Harry," worked with director Don Siegel again on "The Beguiled," and made his directorial debut with "Play Misty For Me." Sam Peckinpah's "Straw Dogs" and Ken Russell's "The Devils" still touch nerves — they're movies you couldn't make today. "Wake in Fright" and "Walkabout" catalyzed an Australian New Wave, and "Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song" and "Shaft" helped revolutionize Black-led cinema. We haven't even touched "Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory" or "A Touch of Zen." Great filmmaking was everywhere in 1971. It's astonishing that what are now classic movies were all released in 2007, a 20-year span that makes this year stand out from the crowd. First and foremost, there's "No Country For Old Men," one of the best movies of the century, which finally won the Coen Brothers Best Picture. On the flip side, there's "There Will Be Blood," one of Paul Thomas Anderson's many masterpieces. David Fincher's "Zodiac" underperformed at the time but is now often considered perhaps his best work. Andrew Dominik's "The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford" reconceives the Western as a hushed, gorgeous elegy. With "Michael Clayton" and "Juno" rounding out the Best Picture field, the Academy Awards were a murderer's row this year. And then there are the other highlights: "3:10 to Yuma," "Hot Fuzz," "Superbad," "The Darjeeling Limited," and, of course, one of Pixar's funniest and most resonant films, "Ratatouille," which also kicked off the company's boldest and most daring phase of films. No year in the 21st century has topped 2007 in influence and richness of great cinema. 1999 is famously known as the great movie year, so it's no surprise it tops our list, but the release catalog is really just that insane. "The Matrix" completely rewired people's brains. "Fight Club" bombed at the box office before becoming a defining text of the DVD era. People dodged conversations about "The Sixth Sense" left and right to preserve the twist. "The Blair Witch Project" pioneered new internet-era movie marketing. "American Beauty" took over the adult drama market and went on to win Best Picture. Paul Thomas Anderson indulged himself with the sprawling and operatic "Magnolia." Stanley Kubrick's final film, "Eyes Wide Shut," arrived posthumously. Audiences uniformly tried to convince themselves they liked "Star Wars: The Phantom Menace," and Pixar earned praise for its first sequel, "Toy Story 2." I don't know how else to fit the breadth of what came out this year in this without just listing it all: "The Virgin Suicides," "Election," "The Insider," "Bringing Out the Dead," "Ghost Dog: The Way of the Samurai," "The Straight Story," "Beau Travail," "Audition," "Office Space," "American Pie," "10 Things I Hate About You," "Dogma," and "South Park: Bigger, Longer, and Uncut." At the cusp of the new millennium, Hollywood, international studios, and indie filmmakers all around were making movies like it was the end of the world. Who knows if we'll ever have a year quite this stacked ever again.

A retail worker discovered $1,300 tucked inside an envelope that looked like trash. That money could’ve helped them plenty, but keeping it never truly felt like an option. Read on to see where the cash ended up. Three years back, my niece came to live with me after her mom and stepdad moved out of state. The understanding was that she’d stay behind and live with me while they relocated. I agreed to let her live with my wife and I without paying rent or other expenses. The formal agreement was that she would prioritize college and work toward some kind of educational or career goal. I didn’t care what major. This man doesn’t see any real progress from his niece. However, that didn’t happen. She didn’t enroll in school at the time, and for the past three years, she hasn’t taken any visible steps toward a degree. She does have a job and pays for her own phone plan and luxuries, but I cover all housing-related costs. Recently, she mentioned she’s taking some classes, but I haven’t seen any evidence of this. She doesn’t bring it up, and conversations are usually about work or our news, but not school. Explicitly asking gets me generic replies. He also has an issue with her poor living habits. The bigger issue, though, is her living habits. Her room is extremely messy. I’ve found trash (like a disposable spork) outside her door. And when I get a look inside, I can’t even see the floor through all the clothes and boxes. I’ve asked her multiple times to clean it, and she always says she will, but nothing changes. My wife has also tried talking to her, with no success. Her niece refused to move back to her mom’s place. When her mom talked to her about moving back, my niece refused. She said she felt abandoned because my sister chose to move out of state. Despite choosing to remain in our home state and city, her feelings are valid. But I don’t think that is fair to my sister that my niece claims she was abandoned. So now, he’s thinking about being frank with her that she needs to move out. At this point, my wife and I both feel that it’s time for her to move out. I’m offering her two clear options. She can live with her mom and stepdad, or with her dad and his wife. But I don’t think she can continue living here when there’s no real plan, progress, or respect for the space. So, WIBTA if I told her it’s time to move out and choose between living with her mom or her dad? I’m not trying to be cruel, but I don’t think this arrangement is healthy or fair anymore. Doing the right thing isn’t always easy, but this employee definitely made the right decision. I hope the woman realizes where she left it and comes back for it. In a market that is possibly the least affordable it has ever been (thanks to enterprise demand), it's virtually impossible to invest in traditional upgrades. Switching to a new GPU or CPU platform has been prohibitively expensive for almost a year now. People have to think twice even before expanding their NVMe storage. This makes PCIe expansion cards possibly the cheapest PC upgrades in 2026. Your motherboard's PCIe x1 slot has most likely been gathering dust all these years, but it can deliver disproportionate returns. For less than $50, you can upgrade your old PC's networking, audio, or I/O hardware with a compact yet effective expansion card. Your free PCIe slots hold a lot of promise If you were in the market for a graphics card or a DDR5 upgrade back in September 2025, you probably remember that things were a lot different than they are right now. Ever since the enterprise demand for AI chips skyrocketed, RAM prices went through the roof and slowly pushed GPU and SSD prices to new highs. Upgrade plans were shelved across the globe as people buckled in for half a decade of insane hardware prices. If you already have an RTX 30 series GPU or anything newer, you can easily ride this crisis out. Most games, even AAA titles, don't need the latest GPUs to push playable framerates. Upscaling, unofficial frame generation, and optimized settings make 6-year-old GPUs pretty powerful. And upgrading to a Ryzen 7000, Ryzen 9000, or Intel Arrow Lake CPU won't feel drastically different than your 5-year-old CPU, at least for gaming. Even SSD prices are crazy right now, with a 2TB Gen4 NVMe drive going for at least $250. Compared to September 2025, that's more than double the price. So, it's safe to say that the non-conventional parts of your old PC deserve some attention at this time. Your unused PCIe x1 slot promises some practical and highly affordable upgrades that can make your system feel modern without blowing a hole in your wallet. Focus on the essentials while you wait for PC hardware prices to fail The tiny PCIe x1 slot near the bottom of your motherboard might not be on your list of upgrades, but it can be surprisingly useful. It can't compete in bandwidth with the full-sized PCIe x16 or even PCIe x8 slots, but it doesn't need to. Depending on the age of your PC, you may have a PCIe 3.0 x1 or PCIe 4.0 x1 slot, which means at least 8 Gbps of bandwidth. This is more than enough for most expansion cards you can buy. For instance, your old PC probably has a dated Ethernet port capped at 1 GbE or 2.5 GbE. If you need more throughput for your internal transfers, this probably doesn't cut it. Fortunately, a 5 GbE Ethernet card only needs a PCIe 3.0 x1 slot to supercharge your PC's wired networking chops, and it costs just $30. If you have a PCIe 4.0 x1 slot, you can even install a 10 GbE PCIe card for around $50. If your motherboard doesn't have onboard Wi-Fi, you can add a PCIe Wi-Fi card for about $25–$35. They feature dedicated, high-gain antennas for a reliable wireless connection when a wired network isn't possible. Many users run out of SATA ports on their motherboard once they've plugged in enough hard drives and SATA SSDs. With a PCIe SATA card, you can introduce additional SATA ports for $20–$35, depending on the number of ports. Similarly, PCIe USB cards can give you extra USB-A and USB-C ports for just $15–$30. 1080p capture cards and PCIe sound cards are also available for less than $25, and can be useful in the right scenario. You don't need constant hardware upgrades.  As you might know, PCIe cards aren't the only way to add new features to your motherboard. You can use a spare M.2 slot as well to add a Wi-Fi, SATA, NVMe, or USB card. However, having an unused M.2 slot is far less likely than having a PCIe one. On top of that, PCIe slots have certain advantages over M.2 slots when it comes to adding larger, high-bandwidth expansion cards. Your PCIe x1 slot is limited in bandwidth, but larger PCIe x4 and x8 slots have up to 128 Gbps of bandwidth on the PCIe 4.0 bus. In contrast, an M.2 slot with a PCIe 4.0 x3 configuration has about 64 Gbps of bandwidth. For a second GPU, an HBA card, or a multi-SSD NVMe adapter, the PCIe slot clearly beats an M.2 one. Second, your PCIe x8 and x16 slots can deliver up to 75W of power compared to 5–10W from an M.2 slot. This makes your PCIe slots more versatile than M.2 slots. Even the PCI x1 slot is capable of a maximum of 25W, although most x1 cards don't need that much power. Lastly, since PCIe expansion cards have a larger footprint than M.2 cards, passive cooling is more efficient when you're installing a PCIe card. An M.2 card cramped below your large GPU can sometimes thermal throttle and hurt performance. Add more speedy storage with those unused slots. Since most PCs only ever use the primary x16 slot for the graphics card, the remaining PCIe slots are forgotten. The smallest PCIe x1 slot is the unluckiest of the bunch, since it's often assumed to be too slow for upgrades. However, most expansion cards that you need fit perfectly within the bandwidth limits of the PCIe x1 slot. It provides you with one of the cheapest ways to augment your PC's capabilities. Practicing Timeless Virtue in Thought, Word, & Deed  By: Brett and Kate McKay  October 25, 2026 In: Social, Social Skills  You’ve talked to a cute barista at your favorite coffee shop for months, but you only see her when she’s working. You’ve become good buddies with a guy at work, but you’ve never hung out with him outside the office. You really enjoy chatting with a dude at church, but you’ve never moved beyond making small talk on Sundays. A lot of men bemoan the less-than-robust nature of their romantic and social lives, but the truth is, they haven’t done much to change them. These men are reactive instead of proactive, hoping that someone else will make the first move instead. Yet other people are in the very same passive mindset. Thus, nobody gets together with anybody! If you want to make progress in your social life, it’s up to you to break this stalemate by taking the initiative yourself. You do that by inviting people you want to get to know better to do things — to go on a date or hang out. Of course, the reason the majority of people don’t take the initiative is that doing so is risky — you worry your invitations will come out weird and that your friendly entreaties will be rejected. Fortunately, it’s easy to make invitations in ways that significantly reduce any potential awkwardness, and greatly increase their chances of being accepted. Just follow these tips Alan Garner lays out in Conversationally Speaking: Keep a dual perspective. Don’t assume people share all your interests, and simply invite them to do something you think is fun. Instead, find out what activities they like, and invite them to do something you both enjoy. By maintaining this “dual perspective,” you’ll be more likely to get a yes. Be specific and direct. How many times do you run into an acquaintance and the conversation ends with this exchange: “We should hang out sometime,” followed by their response, “Yeah definitely.” Of course, neither one of you sees the other until you randomly run into each other again, only to repeat your vague intentions of getting together “sometime.” Instead of making hazy, indefinite invitations, be specific and direct. Ask someone if they want to do X activity, at X place, on X day, at X time. Ask a yes or no question, and get a yes or no answer. Don’t ask: “Are you doing anything Saturday night?” Garner explains why: Many people (and I am one) feel embarrassed at responding, ‘No I’m not doing anything at all.’ And having said that, some feel resentful at being put into the position of having to either agree to the proposal, offer another, or say in effect that they’d rather do nothing than be with you. Start small. People are more likely to say yes to an invitation that requires a minimal commitment. So instead of inviting someone to an elaborate, multi-hour affair, propose meeting up at the gym for a workout or for drinks after work. On the romantic front, instead of asking someone out to dinner, ask if she’ll join you for coffee. A coffee date is accordion-like in its structure: if it goes poorly, you can keep it short and depart after 20 minutes or so. If it goes very well, you can expand it further and ask if she’d like to go do something else. “What’s the rest of your morning look like? Do you want to go check out the farmer’s market?” Sound casual. The tone of your invitation will influence its recipient’s response. The sound of anxiety and desperation reads as low status; it sends a visceral signal that you’re going to be a negative burden in their life rather than a positive asset. To which of these invitations would you respond more positively: Don’t imbue your invitations with heavy, life or death stakes. Keep ’em light, casual, and confident. Invite the person to do something you were going to do anyway. Your tone should be: “I think you’d have fun doing this. But if you don’t want to go, that’s okay by me. No big deal.” If you get a no . . . What if you follow the tips above, but the person still says no to your invitation? If he or she says no, but proposes another time — “I can’t make it this Saturday, but how about the next?” — then they likely reciprocate your interest (platonic or romantic) in getting to know each other better. If they say they can’t make it, but don’t propose another time, then they’re not likely interested in hanging out. Still, try extending an invitation again a few weeks later. If you get the same response (a no without an attempt to propose another time), then you can feel more certain that they’re not interested. There are exceptions of course, and the firmness of this guideline applies more to asking for dates (it’s essentially the Brad Pitt rule) than asking platonic acquaintances to hang out. In the latter case, if you keep running into each other and having good conversations in which the other person expresses what seems like sincere interest in hanging out, you might consider extending a third or even fourth invite. Well spaced out, of course. Some people are just flaky, and really poor initiative takers, or just passing through a busy phase in their lives, and need multiple invitations before they’ll say yes. Read their tone, and parse their words, in deciding how persistent to be. If you determine that that particular person doesn’t wish to hang out, no worries. Now that you know how to make non-awkward, easily accepted invitations, you can start regularly offering them to the many other fish in the sea! AMD Director of Client Product Management Travis Kirsch sat down with a Japanese publication to share the backstory of the AMD Ryzen 7 5800X3D and its relaunch this year. Kirsch told MyNavi Tech+ [machine translated] that AMD CEO Lisa Su was one of the proponents of bringing back the groundbreaking X3D processor that first debuted in April 2022.       While some may think this was a simple relaunch of a four-year-old processor, the company had to do extensive re-engineering and update its manufacturing process with TSMC just to bring it back. The decision to relaunch it was well-timed, too. While the world is suffering from extremely high DDR5 memory prices when it finally arrived in the middle of 2026, Kirsch said that “this was planned before changes in the memory market occurred, not as a countermeasure to DDR5 shortages,” and that it was “the final gift to local users who have used our AM4 for nearly a decade, offering systems that use DDR4 the last change to upgrade their PCs.” Beyond the Ryzen 7 5800X3D, the Japanese publication also touched on AMD’s value offerings, or lack thereof. Four Ryzen 3 processors are available new today—one for AM5 and three for AM4—which raises the question of whether AMD is abandoning the entry-level market. As for the affordable CPU market, he said it’s no longer as big as it used to be, as laptops have taken over this segment. Officers baton-charge demonstrators in overnight operation as activists demand government action on soaring rents and home shortages. Save Share Police in Portugal have cleared a camp in central Lisbon set up to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, baton-charging demonstrators and making 25 arrests. Dozens of officers, some with police dogs, moved in on the camp in Rossio Square shortly after 2am (02:00 GMT) on Sunday. They had warned protesters that their tents would be dismantled if they were not removed, threatening disobedience charges for those who resisted. Protesters had pitched more than 100 tents after Saturday’s protest march by thousands along one of Lisbon’s main avenues. A smaller camp of about 50 tents was also dismantled in Porto’s Praca D Joao I public square, where police made six arrests. Police said the operation was “proportionate” and that the 25 people arrested in Lisbon were later released and are due in court on Monday. While police reported seven minor injuries among officers and protesters in the two operations, the activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 people were hurt and called for a fresh protest outside parliament on Tuesday. “Choosing the early hours of the morning to unleash dogs and baton-charge peaceful protesters is a political decision. It shows this government would rather repress those denouncing the housing crisis than address it,” the group said. Portugal is grappling with one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, as prices have more than doubled since 2017 while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, with young people among the hardest hit. Protesters say soaring rents and higher living costs are squeezing households and turning housing into a growing source of discontent.      The Bank of Portugal estimates a shortfall of 300,000 homes nationwide, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock. The protesters are demanding that the government scrap a bill to make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first parliamentary reading, although the far-right Chega party abstained. The protests in Portugal echo recent demonstrations in Spain over home shortages and surging rents. There have also been protests in cities including Paris, where small student demonstrations over school conditions broadened into wider protests against government economic policies. India’s 2029 rear-crash rule could cost car makers ₹2,700 crore annually, squeeze small-car margins India’s April 2029 rear-impact safety mandate could add approximately ₹2,700 crore annually to passenger vehicle manufacturing costs, as automakers strengthen rear structures, fuel-system protection and electric-vehicle battery safeguards. An illustrative calculation by industry experts tracking the development estimated additional costs of ₹5,000 per small car, ₹4,000 for conventional SUVs and sedans, and ₹15,000 for electric and hybrid vehicles, based on annual vehicle sales of around five million units. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways’ notification S.O. 5723(E), dated October 19 and published on October 21, applies AIS-101 Revision 1, as amended, to covered passenger vehicles from April 1, 2029. Hatchbacks and compact sedans may require reinforced rear cross-members, stronger fuel-tank brackets, protective fuel-line shielding and revised filler-pipe routing. Rear floor panels could also need strengthening, according to automotive engineers. At an assumed 35 per cent market share, small cars would incur an estimated ₹875 crore annually in additional costs. The projected ₹5,000 increase per vehicle represents roughly 0.83 to 1 per cent of the price of a ₹5-6 lakh car. As Sudan’s war destroys livelihoods and pushes people towards artisanal mining, the death of 16-year-old Altayeb Alhadi highlights the dangers facing young workers in an industry offering little protection. Save Share When Altayeb Alhadi was just six years old, his father died after a well collapsed in his village in White Nile state, south-central Sudan. Two months later, his mother also died, leaving the five children in the family as orphans. As the eldest of the siblings, it was Altayeb’s responsibility to find work and help the family survive. At 14, he travelled hundreds of kilometres from his home in Galli village to seek work in the north, where gold mines dot the landscape, so he could feed his siblings and keep them in school. “We warned him about the dangers, but he was ambitious. Some relatives were already working in the area although they had found jobs in restaurants and other services rather than underground extraction,” Ayateb’s uncle Alhadi Hamid told Al Jazeera. The boy initially worked in transport and other jobs, but when he heard lucrative stories from miners in the area, he began to search for gold in the surrounding mountains. Altayeb died in an air strike attributed to the Egyptian military at a gold-mining site near Jabal Al-Aigdat in Sudan’s Red Sea region on October 10, which killed at least 72 miners, a few months after he began working at the site. “It was less than 30 minutes since we separated, and he said he was going to the mine. We suddenly heard a loud sound of bombardment, and we ran. It was too chaotic with people running in all directions and many attacks taking place within a few minutes,” a fellow miner told Al Jazeera, speaking on condition of anonymity. “We found Altayeb with his hand and leg [blown off] and a severe injury to his abdomen [which] was open. We tried to help him and took him to a safer place near a mountain. We were terrified. He died within hours. … We couldn’t believe how quickly things could happen.” Altayeb worked alongside about 15 young men and children, using basic tools to extract gold from the rocks. The miners worked night and day, taking the material they gathered to nearby mills for processing. Proceeds from any gold found were shared, but earnings depended on the amount of gold recovered and individual agreements. On productive days, the group could earn more than $100, the miner said. “We used to dig for two to three weeks until we found a gram or less. If the gold percentage in the well wasn’t good, we would change locations. When we found a gram or less, we sold it and shared the profit, which was about $100,” Altayeb’s former colleague said. For young people supporting relatives, even irregular earnings in these dangerous gold mines can seem preferable to unemployment. Altayeb told his siblings 10 days before his death that he would soon return home, his sister Rogaia Alhadi told local media. Friends told the family that Altayeb visited them at a restaurant near the mining site on the morning of the attack, his uncle said. They shared a cup of tea before heading towards the mine for the final time. Minutes later, the air strike hit the area. Authorities in Egypt have accused Sudanese miners of crossing its border and reportedly linked some to gold smuggling, drugs and human trafficking. The Sudanese side did not respond to these allegations. Since a civil war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group broke out in 2023, the economy has tanked and forced thousands with no other source of income to find work in the artisanal gold mines of northern Sudan. This can vary from independent prospecting to working in investor-owned pits for a share of the proceeds. Earnings depend on the amount of gold found, equipment and fuel costs, and profit percentages agreed with financiers. Although some miners strike gold, they still face an array of dangers, ranging from collapsing shafts and unstable ground to air strikes. Limited medical care makes mining, particularly in remote areas, especially hazardous. Living conditions are also extremely hard. Mohamed Awadalkarim, who was a miner in River Nile state for 10 years, said workers often shelter in makeshift huts made from burlap sacks and plastic sheeting. Their diet consists mainly of lentils and sorghum porridge. But for families without reliable incomes, mining offers a possible source of immediate earnings. Miners may spend hours searching for gold and not find enough to cover their expenses. Others share proceeds with investors or equipment owners, leaving them with limited money left. Artisanal and small-scale mining accounted for 53.71 tonnes, or about 83 per cent, of Sudan’s declared gold production in 2024, but this was just in areas under government control, according to research by the Chatham House think tank. About one million people were involved in artisanal mining across Sudan’s 18 states, generating $1bn annually for the country. Artisanal mines, while generally viewed as being outside the main war-funding networks, have still been exposed to violence. On June 16, several people were reportedly killed and injured in attacks on mining sites near the Egyptian border, according to local sources and miners. The repeated air strikes near Sudan’s border with Egypt have raised concerns about civilian protection, territorial sovereignty and accountability. Egyptian authorities have accused Sudanese prospectors of crossing the border to mine near a concession managed by an Egyptian company, but there is little independent evidence to back these claims. Sudanese military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan reportedly ordered a fact-finding committee involving prosecutors, judicial representatives and security agencies to investigate the attack. Findings from an inquiry into a similar incident announced in June have not been made public. Altayeb paid the highest price in this regional conflict and the hunt for gold, which provides huge profits for some and meagre incomes for many. Altayeb’s siblings are now living with their extended family, including uncles, aunts and cousins. People who know them are trying to help his brothers and sisters and are carrying out community initiatives in Galli to keep his memory alive. “We will raise the children and care for them as he would have wanted. He was young, caring and brave, and he will always be remembered,” Altayeb said.          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Maybe Apple's idea wasn't such a great one after all. Reading time: 4 minutes Abhijeet Mishra / SamMobile Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 It wasn't easy for Apple to enter the foldable market eight years late and prove it had good reasons to avoid it all this time. Apple went above and beyond to make the iPhone Duo stand out because it had to.  However, some are starting to wonder if Apple went too far just to make a point. Samsung took notice of these complaints on social media and jumped on the opportunity to enhance its brand's visibility among iPhone fans.  A recent TechDroider post compared the anti-reflection properties of the iPhone Duo and the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 side by side. The Fold 8 was the clear anti-reflection winner despite Apple's efforts, and Samsung Mobile U.S. cheekily replied on X: Thanks for shedding some light on this 😎.  @techdroider Thanks for shedding some light on this 😎 — Samsung Mobile US (@SamsungMobileUS) October 23, 2026 — Samsung Mobile US (@SamsungMobileUS) October 23, 2026   Upon releasing the iPhone Duo eight years after Samsung's first Fold, Apple really tried to come in strong and make a statement. In an interview with TIME, the new CEO, John Ternus, even described existing foldable phones as feeling “kind of cheap and crappy.“  By the way, those words seem to have already aged like milk after the iPhone Duo utterly failed the same independent durability tests that the Fold 8 had passed.  But back to the topic, one way Apple tried to make the iPhone Duo stand out was by disguising the notorious crease better than its competitors. To this end, the iPhone Duo became the first iPhone to use Apple's Nano Texture display finish.  What is Apple's Nano Texture?  It's the name Apple gave to its display etching technology. Nano Texture panels have microscopic ridges that scatter light rather than reflect it. Instead of seeing crisp reflections on the iPhone Duo's screen, Nano Texture softens and scatters them across a larger area in a softer gradient.  At least, that's the theory. The idea seems sound, especially because Nano Texture already has fans among Apple MacBook and monitor users. It can be useful in an office environment where you might not be able to move your PC or adjust your workspace when the sun starts shining into your monitor.  However, there may be a good reason why Apple has never used Nano Texture on an iPhone, or why MacBook, iPad, and Apple monitor users are always given a choice between a glossy display finish and Nano Texture. iPhone Duo users don't have that choice. It's either Nano Texture or a different phone.  That's starting to be a problem. As seen recently on social media, more and more early iPhone Duo adopters are now finding out that the Nano Texture layer can do more harm than good. When hit with a powerful light source, the iPhone Duo's Nano Texture arguably scatters too much light, leading to a blurry, low-contrast look that can't match the Fold 8 screen's crispness and deep contrast.  A couple of other unpleasant byproducts inherent to the iPhone Duo's Nano Texture are:    All in all, the Galaxy Z Fold 8's inner screen looks better, and iPhone Duo users who were brave enough to peel the Nano Texture layer off also found that the Fold 8's screen looks flatter.  Samsung is clearly in a winning position here, especially considering the mismanaged, delayed iPhone Duo launch in most markets.  As for Nano Texture, maybe there is a good reason Apple has never applied this finish to an iPhone screen before the Duo. And given Samsung's experience in display and foldable phone manufacturing, the Korean tech giant may have known about these shortcomings long before Apple.  Keep in mind that Samsung Display manufactures the iPhone Duo's foldable panel. However, the Nano Texture idea that doesn't seem to be working too well for the iPhone Duo was Apple's. By   	Essie Assibu   	As the ninth edition of El Gouna Film Festival wrapped in Egypt, the conversation among some of the country’s and region’s leading producers and filmmakers turned to what the industry needs to turn its wealth of talent into films that can find audiences both at home and abroad.  	Egyptian cinema once dominated film production across the Arab world, but output fell dramatically from its late-20th-century heights. According to figures from the Egyptian Chamber of Cinema Industry, the country produced 112 films in 1988, before output fell to just 16 a decade later. More recently, production has shown signs of recovery, rising from 51 feature films in 2022 to 67 in 2023.  	            	 	 		 					Related Stories		 	               	 		 					'Crazy Rich Asians' HBO Series Sets Cast: Constance Wu, Henry Golding, Michelle Yeoh, Ronny Chieng Returning		 			               	 		 					Iberseries Takeaways: Woody Allen on His New Film, Los Javis Pact With HBO Max, the Tales of Cachou the Brown Bear and More		 			         	For veteran Syrian producer Mohamed Mashish, who has built a decades-long career in Egypt, capitalizing on that momentum starts with the screenplay.     			Popular on Variety		       	“We need to have more time for development and scriptwriting,” he tells Variety. “We have all the industry components. But we don’t have scripts. So what can you do? I have a nice camera, a good DP, but we can’t do anything without good scripts.”  	Mashish has seen firsthand how new platforms can expand the reach of Egyptian storytelling. He produced the 2016 drama “Grand Hotel,” which became the first Egyptian and first Arabic-language series to land on Netflix when the streamer released it internationally as “Secret of the Nile” in 2018.  	He believes younger filmmakers are also benefiting from greater access to work from around the world. “They’re more open-minded. They’re connected on the internet and everything,” he notes. “Because the platforms are available now, they’re watching more than just our culture. So they are more open and they are ready to move.”  	           	But Mashish argues that new perspectives need to be matched with experience. “We have to bring the old generation and the new generation together,” he explains. “The new generation brings a different perspective, but cinema still needs experience, so we need to combine that new talent with the expertise that already exists in the industry.”  	Egyptian director Hadi El Bagoury, whose 2016 “Hepta: The Last Lecture” became the highest-grossing romantic film in Egyptian cinema, points to streaming as one of the biggest opportunities for homegrown talent.  	The growth of platforms, he argues, has given filmmakers more places to show their work while exposing audiences to a wider range of filmmaking. “You discover new stories, new directors, new genres,” he says. “You discover a lot more directors, DPs, actors and different styles.”  	That exposure is also changing what audiences expect from Egyptian cinema. “They want new genres, they want original stories,” El Bagoury says.  	The shift has particular consequences in the Gulf, a crucial market for Egyptian films. Mashish points to Saudi Arabia’s theatrical expansion as an example of how quickly audiences have evolved.  	“At the beginning, when the Saudis started to open cinemas, they accepted everything because it was new,” he recalls. “It’s like, ‘I will go to the cinema, I will have popcorn, no matter the kind of movie I will watch.'”  	“They are more selective than before,” he continues. “They will not accept just anything coming anymore. Because cinemas are now open in Saudi and in the Gulf, they are watching international cinema. So they demand this kind of quality.”  	For Lebanese producer and distributor Ziad Srouji (“Palestine 36”), whose career spans film and television across the Arab world, reaching audiences beyond the region does not mean making Arab films resemble foreign ones.  	“Specificity travels; generic does not,” he stresses. “International buyers aren’t looking for Arab films that imitate Western genre cinema, and they’re tired of films made only to explain the region to outsiders. They want stories rooted in a very particular world but driven by a premise anyone can grasp in one sentence.”  	For Srouji, the challenges often come after the initial idea. “A good idea gets you into the room. It doesn’t get you through production, and it certainly doesn’t get you to an audience.”  	           	The bigger obstacles, he believes, are often structural. “Too many films reach the market without a sales agent attached early, without delivery materials ready and without a positioning strategy beyond a festival premiere,” Srouji says. “Sales and distribution need a strategy built from day one, not after the premiere.”  	El Gouna is among the regional festivals trying to strengthen the path from development onward. CineGouna, its industry arm, launched the Egyptian Voices strand this year, selecting four Egyptian projects in development for tailored training in pitching, packaging and co-production.  	El Bagoury argues that the industry also needs more ways to reach audiences directly. “We need more Egyptian-owned platforms, more theaters. Theaters that are cheap, accessible to all,” he says. “We need a lot of this so we don’t have to depend on anybody else. We need to show our films in our cinemas and on our platforms.”  	For Srouji, the ultimate measure of a healthy industry is not simply whether a filmmaker gets a movie made or lands a prestigious festival selection, but whether that success makes the next film possible.  	“A major festival selection is a launch, not a career,” he says. “Sustainable success is when your second film is easier to finance than your first.” The Business of Entertainment

CrystalDiskInfo has been synonymous with SSD and HDD monitoring for years. It reads your drive's Self-Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Technology (S.M.A.R.T.) attributes and presents them on a single screen for easy reference. Checking your SSD's health percentage, temperature, or other metrics is pretty simple with this free tool.  However, you don't really need to install a third-party tool if all you need to know is your SSD health and temperature. SSDs have a limited lifespan due to the finite write cycles of NAND flash, so most people only need to know their drive's remaining life. And Windows' built-in storage settings are more than enough for that. Windows can maintain your SSD really well, but it sure makes you work for those features Every drive, whether it's an HDD or SSD, has a reserved area to store its S.M.A.R.T. data. This data is persistent across reboots, power cycles, and host machine changes. It is this data that the OS or third-party software queries and displays to the user. S.M.A.R.T. data is the primary source to monitor a drive's remaining health or diagnose underlying faults. Most users don't know this, but you don't need extra tools to see your SSD's S.M.A.R.T. attributes. Windows already has an easy way to glance at your drive's Estimated remaining life, Available spare, and Temperature attributes. All you need to do is navigate to Settings > System > Storage > Disks & volumes and click Properties under the SSD you want to check.  The Estimated remaining life is the same as the oft-used "SSD health" metric, which indicates how much of your SSD's estimated lifespan is over. It's only a rough prediction based on the NAND flash wear of your drive, so it doesn't guarantee that your SSD will work perfectly until this attribute goes to zero. Available spare refers to the reserve NAND blocks on your SSD that it uses once the active blocks start to fail. Most people will see a 95–100% reading here, which means the SSD hasn't dipped into its spare capacity at all. Lastly, Temperature shows the current temperature of your SSD. This Properties page of your SSD is enough to give you almost all the information you need to get a rough indication of your SSD's health. A couple of tweaks can quietly extend the remaining lifespan of your drive While Windows shows you the estimated remaining life of your SSD and the available spare capacity, that's not the whole picture. Even your SSD's 100% health doesn't guarantee that everything is hunky-dory underneath. All you can really say with certainty is that you've written 5% of your SSD's rated write capacity, also known as the TBW rating (terabytes written). NAND flash wear, however, is just one possible pathway to SSD failure. Naturally, SSD health doesn't take into account unexpected power, thermal, or firmware-related faults that can kill your SSD years before you're even close to exhausting your TBW rating. What you need to investigate is whether your SSD has had any drive write errors in the past. Windows doesn't show you that information; you need CrystalDiskInfo for that.  CrystalDiskInfo's Media and Data Integrity Errors and Critical Warning attributes show the true picture of your SSD. The former is a log of the instances when your SSD's error-correction mechanism failed to fix a read or write error, indicating the presence of faulty cells. The latter takes into account other attributes to signal to the user that the drive demands urgent attention. Most SSDs don't begin to have data integrity errors years into their life, so Windows' built-in information is sufficient for most users. However, if your SSD is showing symptoms of underlying faults, it's best to use CrystalDiskInfo to inspect the metrics not exposed by Windows' storage settings. The reasons might be hiding under your nose If you spot a non-zero entry next to Media and Data Integrity Errors or Critical Warning in CrystalDiskInfo and your SSD has been finicky of late, you need to prepare for the worst. The first order of business is to try software fixes like CHKDSK to fix minor faults. If that doesn't work, it's time to move your data off the drive by backing it up to a healthy drive. Your faulty SSD can be repurposed into a non-critical system or let go entirely. In this market, replacing your SSD with a new one won't be easy on your wallet. Prices of NVMe SSDs have increased by 3–4 times compared to September 2025, so you'll have to be flexible. SATA SSDs are cheaper and still fast enough for gaming and regular system operations for most people. You could even look at used SATA SSDs as long as you can inspect them before buying.  If you want an NVMe SSD anyway, avoid Gen5 drives and pick an affordable Gen4 model. I'd suggest looking for a deal on a 2TB Gen4 SSD, which could get you a decent drive for around $250. A 1TB model will be too small for most people, and the cost per GB will also be higher. You're paying for sequential speeds which don't matter in game Whether your SSD is faulty or not depends on a lot more factors than a single health percentage. That's only a rough estimate of how much data you've written to your drive. Most people won't kill their SSD in a few years, so Windows is still sufficient to measure your drive's health. If you're facing storage-related errors on your PC, however, try CrystalDiskInfo to find out more about your drive and whether you need to replace it. We want to hear from you. The former US president warns of rising costs, corruption and threats to democratic values ahead of the November 3 vote. Save Share Obama joins El-Sayed in Michigan rally cry before key midterms Former President Barack Obama has railed against the Trump administration on a range of issues, including dragging the United States into “an unnecessary war” against Iran, as he campaigned for Democrats in Ohio and Michigan ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Speaking at rallies on Saturday, Obama accused President Donald Trump of “chaos and corruption”, as he urged voters to reject Republicans. The speeches came just 10 days before the elections, with Senate and gubernatorial races taking place in both states. Here are the key takeaways: “The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said in Cleveland, Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. “Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for,” Obama said. The former president defended the 2015 nuclear agreement reached under his administration, which restricted Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. “Iran didn’t have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place that everybody acknowledged kept them from getting nukes, and I didn’t have to fire a missile to do it. I just had to engage in diplomacy,” Obama said. “He pulled out of it, starts this war.” Obama blamed the conflict for rising oil and diesel prices, citing attacks on US military bases, American casualties and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. “Our allies and our bases have been attacked. Americans have been killed, hundreds of Americans have been wounded. We have run down our stock of missiles, and Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz where oil goes through to the world market,” he said. The disruptions in oil flow through the strait, located between Iran and Oman, have pushed up energy prices worldwide. Before the war, a fifth of global oil and gas passed through the strait, which Iran has used as leverage in the war. “This is the reason why the price of oil is up … This is the reason the price of diesel is up.” The spike in diesel and petrol prices will likely cost the Republican Party, as the majority of Americans hold Trump responsible for starting the war and the subsequent increase in prices. Obama also mocked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his focus on military culture and the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. “These are not serious people,” Obama said. Obama criticised Trump’s tariffs, saying Americans were paying more for goods, including products made in the US using imported parts. “When you impose tariffs, consumers pay the tab,” he said. “It’s not just the goods that you use directly that have been imported … It’s also the car you build here in America. They might need a part from somewhere else, and now suddenly there’s a tariff on it.” He questioned Trump’s trade dispute with Canada, a major US trading partner. The two countries have been locked in a trade dispute, with Trump threatening 50 percent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts from January 2027. “And the big trade war he’s starting now is with that well-known evil empire Canada,” Obama said sarcastically. “Canadians are the nicest people … they’re like our friendly neighbours to the north, and he’s like picking a fight with them.” Obama also pointed to the growing US national debt, which has reached $40 trillion. “Instead of bringing down deficits like he said with these tariffs, we’re now running a debt to the tune of $40 trillion.” The figure refers to the total federal debt, which has accumulated over successive administrations, rather than the annual budget deficit. Obama accused the Trump administration of favouring wealthy Americans while common households struggled with rising costs. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,'” Obama declared. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.” He pointed to Trump’s 2025 tax and spending legislation, which extended tax cuts while reducing federal spending on programmes including Medicaid and food assistance. “The only bill they passed of any significance in the last two years was a trillion-dollar tax break that mostly benefitted the richest Americans,” he said. Obama also took aim at Trump’s White House renovations, including plans for a ballroom, changes to the Rose Garden and the addition of gold decorations. “He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama joked. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, just gold everywhere.”  The former president said the US needed secure borders but criticised the methods used by immigration agents under the Trump administration. “I believe that we do need to make sure that our border is orderly and secure and that people who want to come here do so lawfully,” he said. “But I don’t recall anybody campaigning on sending masked agents running through our streets. I don’t recall anybody talking about law-abiding citizens being arrested, detained, or shot.” “That’s not what we have to do to get our borders under control,” he added. In Ohio, Obama criticised Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy over a campaign advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. The advertisement features Acton’s mother questioning her honesty and her account of her childhood, without mentioning the allegations of sexual abuse that led to their separation decades ago. It has drawn criticism from Republicans, including Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, although Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended it. Obama condemned Ramaswamy’s decision to use Acton’s family history in the campaign. “There’s got to be something inside you where you just say, you know, no office is worth stooping that low,” he said. He also praised Acton’s career in public service and urged Ohio voters to support her on November 3.  In Detroit, Obama campaigned for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial contender Jocelyn Benson. He praised El-Sayed’s Michigan roots and criticised his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, over his support for the US-Israel war on Iran and Trump’s trade policies. “Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” Obama said, referring to his upbringing in the state, his family’s ties to the auto industry and his involvement in school sports. Obama also spoke about attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim identity, comparing them with false claims about his own religion and birthplace during his presidential campaigns. “Unlike Mike Rogers, Abdul hasn’t spent months cheerleading the Iran war … or called these tariffs ‘masterful’.” The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a “radical”, declaring that “Abdul shares my values”. Obama also praised Benson for standing by Michigan’s 2020 election results despite threats and protests outside her home. “When armed protesters showed up outside her home in 2020, demanded she overturn Michigan’s fair and free election results, Jocelyn stood her ground, stood up for you and your rights,” he said. Obama said the midterm elections offered voters a chance to limit Trump’s power during the remaining two years of his presidency. “This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said. “It’s the circuit breaker in the system. We need to flip that circuit breaker.” He also warned that dishonesty, intimidation and bullying were becoming accepted in US politics. “We are not going to fix the economic system or the political system … so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes and where people in the highest offices in the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully,” he said. “What we are missing in our public discourse is just basic decency.”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

For the French, everything is coming at once in these difficult weeks.               Thomas Kolbe  |             October 25, 2026           For the French, everything is coming at once in these difficult weeks. After market turmoil, a debt crisis, and migration chaos, gasoline is now running short at many filling stations. President Macron is touring the Middle East in an attempt to secure relief. France is heading toward a historic failure in these weeks. In the country with the world’s largest welfare state, lavish pensions, a state-dominated economy, and the fatal illusion surrounding migration, reality has finally become an immovable wall. At the beginning of the week, another problem emerged for the French: numerous filling stations across the country were experiencing acute shortages of gasoline and diesel. The figures show what the situation at filling stations actually looks like. On Tuesday morning, more than 1,500 stations nationwide were affected by shortages. In eastern France and the Paris region, the share had already exceeded 23 percent. Particularly troubling is the fact that some affected stations could no longer offer their customers any fuel at all. The supply situation is thus becoming an acute risk to mobility and economic activity. Against this backdrop, President Emmanuel Macron has embarked on a three-day trip to the Gulf region. Since Monday, his itinerary has included visits to Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Qatar, with the aim of securing short-term commitments for additional oil and diesel supplies. Macron is accompanied by representatives of the energy companies TotalEnergies and Engie. So far, however, no supply contracts have been concluded. Even though the situation in the Strait of Hormuz has eased in the meantime, it is almost impossible to free up flexible supplies of already-refined fuel from existing delivery contracts. It is therefore unlikely to easily resolve the problem at French filling stations in the short term, particularly since transportation itself would take time. The perfect storm has gathered over France, and the Europeans’ self-deceptions have collided with reality. From the end of fossil fuels to sanctions against Russia, from the lies surrounding migration and multiculturalism to an unlimited welfare state, we are witnessing the collapse of the globalist dream. It appears that the multiple crises are first throwing France into turmoil, shattering the dream of a state-run economy, politically controlled energy flows, and the fragmentation of civil society into cultural sub-identities long envisioned by the Left. Chaos is not a sustainable model of rule. At best, it is the breeding ground for a short-lived and fragile tyranny. Behind the chaos in France, the sovereign debt crisis continues to smolder, having become a threat to the eurozone. As French cities disappear into the smoke of migrant mobs and aggressive far-left milieus, the crisis has developed from a smoldering fire into a raging blaze. After a brief period of calm in the bond market, the yield on France’s ten-year government bond rose again on Wednesday morning, approaching the five-percent mark at a dangerous pace. The European Central Bank appears to have erected an intervention firewall at this threshold. Christine Lagarde stands ready with the money-printing press, prepared, if necessary, to purchase bonds from the market and thereby keep interest rates under control. Can this work in the long run? Bond markets are deep and have enormous capacity. At best, the printing press can deliver a short-term effect, one that must ultimately lead to massive inflation. No, France must solve its debt problem through austerity and a growth-oriented policy -- the era of the socialist feel-good paradise is long over. Marine Le Pen’s announcement that, if elected president, she would shift part of the budgetary burden onto Germany through the CO2 mechanism and a change in membership contributions is dishonest. It signals a rupture in the partnership between Europe’s right-wing parties before that partnership has even had a chance to take hold. There is absolutely no doubt that investors no longer trust the French situation. No one understands how a budget deficit of 5.7 percent can be allowed to persist without any meaningful political reaction. The financing of lavish pensions and the world’s largest welfare system, alongside an official government spending ratio of 57 percent, will also force investors to reassess the situation in light of the chaos in the country. The bottom line: If everything remains as it is -- which seems all too likely -- banks, pension funds, insurers, and hedge funds could send France’s credit rating crashing like a financial guillotine. Stock markets are already reacting to rising interest rates and the persistent selling pressure on French government bonds, and they are moving into a downturn. If the ECB fails to bring interest rates under control, the higher cost of borrowing will gradually feed through the economy’s value chains and financial processes in credit markets: investment and consumer loans will become more expensive. France’s anemic economy would be dealt another heavy blow. They are already acting in a headlong, almost panicked fashion. This would trigger a systemic heart attack and usher in the end of the euro system. The EU’s second-largest pillar could not be kept standing for more than a few weeks, neither through financial transfers from other member states nor through the ECB’s credit pump. In the EU’s capitals, they sense that a decisive phase in the markets may have begun. Fuel reserves are being released. Desperately, they cling to the illusion of victory in the Donbas, all the while keeping their eyes on Russia’s energy and resource reserves and on regime change in the Kremlin. An extremely dangerous situation is taking shape, as politicians in panic mode will no longer act rationally.                    Now more than ever, the ability to speak our minds is crucial to the republic we cherish.
