A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans â including 4 in 10 Republicans â believe thereâs too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this. This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for Californiaâs proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trumpâs sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs. Iâm an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the âmerely wealthy.â Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices â including taxation and public spending â enabled this 40-year rise in inequality. Related Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%. Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow. The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 â and from 27.4% in 1999. These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class â the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% â who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group thatâs 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middleâs share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data. But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth â almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026. Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories. Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall. The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfoliosâ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability thatâs driving up stock prices â especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom. Since President Ronald Reaganâs tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive, often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats. The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research â including international studies â doesnât back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth. Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trumpâs sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940. Itâs also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from. Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%âs wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership, allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways â including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash, usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares. By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%. Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed. One example is a provision in Trumpâs 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs. The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy â while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil. Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%. This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But theyâre not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in âA Brief History of Equality,â published in 2022: âInequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.â  Markus Schneider, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Denver This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Walking into an under-achieving football club is never easy. I know, because I spent my career taking on such challenges. That was the task Michael Carrick took on in January when he was appointed Manchester United's interim manager and took over a club that was drifting deeper and deeper into mediocrity. Supporters talk about seeing a bounce when new managers take over and, from my own experiences, I do believe that to be the case. Michael certainly experienced a fantastic period where results and performances improved. In his case, United's improvement to finish third and in the Champions League places was exceptional - and he also calmed the water behind the scenes. Yet, with every bounce, there almost always comes a return to normality. You see players who raised the level of their performance return to the level they are used to, and everything often slips back to the way it was before. That seems to be what is happening at United now but, while Carrick appears to be under increasing pressure, the club's problems are definitely not just down to who their manager is. Here, I've tried to explain what he needs to do to sort some of his issues out. Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick apologised to the club's 700 travelling supporters for the 4-1 defeat at Como To properly judge Michael, you have to balance up everything he has inherited and consider whether United could be a successful organisation. United have invested enormous amounts of money in recruiting a lot of players in the past five years. Since 2021, they have had three other permanent managers - Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, who spent more than Â£1bn on 27 major signings and many of whom are still at the club. This year, under Michael, they have invested another Â£150m, but the bulk of it was on three midfielders and if you assess his entire squad I would still seriously question how many players he would have chosen out of the group he now has. As a manager going into troubled clubs, you have to immediately set your non-negotiable principles with your players - things like hard work and a collective spirit in the dressing room were imperative for me. You give everyone the same opportunity to jump on board and then quickly recognise the players who are capable of going on the ride with you, and those who can't, or won't. Michael will know all those things about his squad by now, good and bad, but what can he really do about it? In my experience, and I am talking about Premier League clubs, my owners were keen on my views on the players I had just inherited - not just in terms of their ability on the pitch but their value as assets on budget sheets and in the transfer market. I was always continually asked if I could make players better, and also if I could recover money from those I did not rate or want, so as to help the club's financial position. I understood why - my position as manager was to 100% help the club and try to achieve maximum performances on and off the pitch - but it can be hard to do both. It means when you are taking over a group of players your club has invested in, you cannot always be completely honest about certain players in that group. You know the club has a vested interest in holding the player's value and the fact you have to portray positivity to protect that is sometimes unbelievably difficult. Criticising them in the media can't happen, because of your loyalty to the club, so you are left hoping the people who watch your games week in, week out, understand and recognise your dilemma around your squad. The club's recruitment strategy has been publicly questioned recently, of course, by defender Lisandro Martinez - and I am sure a lot of supporters agree with him and/or would like some clarity on that subject. But, from a manager's perspective, Martinez's outburst also raises serious questions about the player himself. Him saying what he did does make me wonder whether he believes he has been a success personally. If so, then how many more players in United's first-team squad also believe themselves to have been successful, rather than part of the problem? Managing players with inflated opinions about themselves is another challenge in itself - and it certainly needs addressing. You can add that to the list of Michael's issues right now, but he has an even bigger problem in how he deals with his captain Bruno Fernandes' comments after United were humbled by Como in the Champions League on Wednesday, Watching Michael in his post-match press conference in Italy was really difficult for me. I've managed games where my team has been beaten while having a right go, but having to see a manager man up to his side after a performance that, for me, questioned their attitude to compete or even run around and try, was heart-wrenching. Listening to the way his captain spoke, after his own example typified his team's reluctance to do the above, it again showed me how difficult it must be at that club at the moment. Michael's tactics are there to be followed, yet to do that away to Como on a very wet and windy miserable night, you need men and not boys. Fernandes seemed to be enjoying his relationship with Carrick last season, when United were flying up the table, but they have now levelled off both as a team and individuals in the way I described in this column. Proper captains, and I was lucky to work with some top guys, come to the fore when the team and club needs them most. I've always judged leaders by people who follow them when things are going wrong. Unfortunately, many members of that team did follow their captain's example, but in a totally unprofessional way. Bruno Fernandes has scored 111 goals in 338 appearances for Manchester United I don't know Michael well, but he was a very honest player who deservedly has great standing at the club he is now managing. I know his backroom staff better - Steve Holland, Jonny Evans and Jonathan Woodgate - and they are all able assistants with knowledge and experience at the very top level. Whenever United are not winning, there will be calls for things to change - and the manager is almost always at the top of that list. So, where should they look now? I believe they should follow the blueprint of one of their great rivals, and realise that continuously changing direction is just not working. When Mikel Arteta arrived at Arsenal in December 2019, he had an instant impact like Michael - not in terms of league position, but by winning the 2020 FA Cup. For a couple of years after that early success, however, Arteta was taking pelters from fans and across the spectrum of media outlets because the upturn in results did not last. Despite that, the club never flinched and gave him the opportunity to install a clear identity throughout the club and also time for it to take shape.  Look where they are now. United have to take their medicine and do similar - they have to understand the consequences of the huge failures in recruitment they have repeatedly made and reset to find a direction and identity again. Time is their biggest challenge there, because everyone demands instant success these days. People, though, have to realise that, while I believe Michael - when everyone is fit - has a group that can still compete for the Champions League places, they are never good enough for the prizes they really want. To be contenders again, they need more than just talent. Ability, pace and character are the characteristics they will need in pretty much every outfield position but, from where they are now, achieving that will not happen quickly. They definitely don't need to change their manager again to get there, however. I was all for Michael getting the job in the first place once Darren Fletcher had been overlooked, and in my humble opinion he should be backed again to do what is needed now. At this moment, United are not capable of winning the league title, whoever is in charge, but stability is the way forward to fix that. Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan. The MacBook Neo was a wake-up call for Windows laptop manufacturers, and showed that you really didn’t need to compromise on the core experiences to deliver a perfectly balanced machine for the vast majority of users. And that kind of still holds true to this day. The MacBook Neo is still one of the best entry level laptops you can find right now, along with newer Windows alternatives such as the 2026 Dell XPS 13. And that's not even taking into account the used marketplace, which has amazing deals if you know where to look. I managed to snag a Dell Latitude 7320 for $600, and it has slowly transformed into my secondary machine in the past week since I bought it. If you're lucky like me, you can get a used business laptop with the specs of a $1,500 laptop for nearly 10% of its price. The mystery laptop in question is a Dell Latitude 7320, a compact and portable powerhouse. It comes equipped with an 11th generation Intel Core i7 (i7-1185G7; vPro variant) that has 4 cores and 8 threads to spare, along with a maximum clock speed of 4.8 GHz. Pair that with one TB of user-replaceable storage and 32 GB of LPDDR4x non-upgradeable RAM, and you have a rather solid laptop. My particular device also has a WWAN slot complete with a modem, although I haven’t been able to use it yet. These Latitudes are also incredibly well-built and can take a beating. While the shell is made of carbon fiber and plastic, it's the sturdy kind of plastic, and will absorb any bumps and bruises along the way. It’s certainly not perfect, and in many ways is starting to show its age (it was released over 5 years ago, after all). Despite that, it is surprisingly capable for basic tasks and sometimes, even a bit extra. The Dell Latitude 7320 is a far more capable laptop, and its port selection is incredibly diverse for such a small form factor. It has two USB-C Thunderbolt-capable ports on either side (both of which support charging), which makes it automatically superior to the MacBook Neo’s dual non-Thunderbolt USB-C ports. If that wasn’t enough of a slam dunk, the Latitude also has a microSD card slot, an HDMI port and a whole USB-A port, which is very much appreciated. It also has a WWAN module, which means you can stick in a SIM card. Combined with an eGPU dock, it makes for a practical and capable desktop replacement that can drive multiple monitors — something the Neo cannot do. It’s incredibly quiet too, even at the maxed out power and fan profiles. Temperatures are quite toasty though, and you have to expect upwards of 90 degrees Celsius during heavy workloads. That being said, the laptop never felt uncomfortably hot to the touch, and the active cooling helps. It also has a few niceties, like a physical webcam shutter and a fingerprint sensor, all of which work under Linux just fine. Speaking of operating systems, this works with both Windows 11 and Linux. I chose Arch Linux, and after installing the relevant Dell driver packages, was able to get things working without any issues. The MacBook Neo is a newer machine, and one that you can still buy in stores with a warranty to go along with it. In case something goes wrong, you’ll be able to take it to the store and have them (or Apple) fix it for you. Used laptops usually do not come with any warranty to speak of, and most safeguards are dubious at best. There’s also the fact that the Dell has an objectively worse display, and by quite a margin. My particular variant isn’t the superior 400-nit version, and is instead relegated to the anemic 250-nit display. Combine that with a rather mediocre built-in panel that exhibits an ungodly amount of ghosting, and you have the worst of both worlds. The Neo’s display is far superior, despite being limited to 60 Hz as well. The Dell laptop also suffers from disappointingly mediocre battery life. I suspect it's a combination of both the smaller 43 Wh battery and the power-hungry CPU (compared to the Neo, which runs on a super efficient mobile chip) that makes it so terrible. It barely lasts 4 hours on a good day, and that's with power savings enabled. To be fair, the MacBook Neo doesn’t offer spectacular battery life either, but It's still a lot better than the Dell. And there’s the fact that you have access to desktop macOS on the MacBook Neo, while you’ll be stuck with Windows 11 on the Dell Latitude. Operating systems are certainly a matter of personal preference, but I’d easily pick the MacBook Neo if it weren’t for its anemic 8 GB of RAM. macOS is just a better operating system, despite its many, many quirks. Honestly speaking? The MacBook Neo is a pretty great deal still and a perfect entry-level laptop, but nothing more. I just wish it had more RAM and a backlit keyboard. Unlike the MacBook Neo, the Dell Latitude 7320 features a lot of upgradeable components. Yes, while the MacBook Neo is still shockingly repairable (for an Apple product), none of its components can be “upgraded”. The storage on the MacBook is soldered, for example. On the Dell, it's as easy as installing a higher capacity M.2 drive later on — you have the ability to choose. It also has a microSD card reader, so you could always make for some extra, cheaper storage. Unfortunately, the RAM is soldered on both laptops, but the Dell variant I have has 32 GB of it, which is more than what I will ever need. The speakers are also a plus, and sound excellent for a Windows laptop. And there’s the whole upgrade path. A lot of these machines ship out with the base spec, and it is possible to swap out most components for a better quality one. The keyboard and battery, for example, can be swapped for backlit and higher-capacity ones, respectively. And this is exactly where business and enterprise laptops shine. They age tremendously well and are a viable alternative for Windows and Linux users. With hardware prices the way they are right now, it's as good a time as any to look into the used market. People across northeastern Nigeria continue searching for loved ones who went missing during years of violence. Save Share Maiduguri, Nigeria – For more than 15 years, Kashim Mohammed has hoped that his younger sister, Falmata Mohammed, is still alive. Falmata disappeared in 2011 while travelling with her mother from Maiduguri, the capital of northeastern Nigeria’s Borno State, to Port Harcourt in the south. According to Kashim, the two women were abducted by unidentified gunmen.     Years later, a man approached Kashim at Baga Road Market in Maiduguri with news that briefly revived the family’s hopes of finding the women. He claimed Falmata had been found in Benin and was searching for her relatives. But the man disappeared without leaving contact details. Kashim said he has never been able to establish whether the information was genuine. “From then until now, nobody knows anything about the man who brought the information,” he said. Kashim, 39, chairs the Association for the Well-being of Displaced and Missing Persons’ Families, a community organisation based in Bolori II, Ngarnam ward, Maiduguri. He said years of violence have torn his family apart. “As a result of the violence, I lost my sister from the same father,” he said. Their father, Mohammed Kolo, worked at Maiduguri’s State Specialist Hospital. Kashim said his father died at 60 from an illness he attributed to high blood pressure without learning what had happened to his daughter. Kolo had refused to abandon hope that she would return. “Our father always said, ‘Wherever she is, I believe my daughter is alive,’” Kashim recalled. For Muhammad Alhaji Bashir, the disappearance of his elder brother, Adam Muhammad Bashir, known as Bakura, has left a similar void. Muhammad, 29, said Bakura went missing around 2012 or 2013 when Muhammad was about 14. His brother, then believed to be in his early 20s, sold cosmetics in a Maiduguri market and was studying civil engineering at Ramat Polytechnic, according to Muhammad. “I sincerely lost my brother as a result of the Boko Haram crisis,” Muhammad said. Boko Haram’s armed rebellion began in northeastern Nigeria in 2009. The conflict has devastated communities through attacks, abductions and displacement, leaving families searching for relatives whose fates remain unknown. Muhammad said Bakura’s family searched across Maiduguri. A rehabilitation centre offered them some hope. “Whenever we heard that rescued people had been brought to the rehabilitation centre in Bulumkutu, we went there with Bakura’s pictures, but unfortunately, nobody recognised him,” Muhammad said. Muhammad said his father and stepmother, who was Bakura’s mother, later died from illnesses the family attributed to hypertension. He and other relatives continue to search, without confirmation of whether Bakura is alive or dead. The two families’ experiences reflect the uncertainty facing relatives of people who have disappeared during more than a decade of conflict in northeastern Nigeria. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), working with the Nigerian Red Cross Society, has supported efforts to trace missing people and reconnect separated families. Local advocates for missing people cited an estimate of 17,000 people missing across northern Nigeria, many of them linked to the conflict involving Boko Haram and its aftermath. Kashim said his association’s records indicated that about 10,000 people are missing in Borno State alone. He added that many families have yet to register their missing relatives. The sources for the estimates cited by advocates and the association, their geographical coverage, reporting periods and methods of compilation have not been independently established for this article. Behind the estimates are families who have spent years searching, parents who have died without learning what happened to their children and children growing up without a parent. Some people reportedly disappeared during attacks on their communities. Others became separated from relatives while fleeing violence or travelling between towns. Families search hospitals, displacement camps and centres receiving people rescued from conflict areas, often following leads that prove impossible to verify. Even when names, photographs and personal details are submitted to organisations involved in tracing missing people, locating relatives can take time. Kashim said his search for Falmata helped motivate him and other affected families to establish their association in 2023. He said the organisation obtained registration with Nigeria’s Corporate Affairs Commission in 2025. Members meet monthly to share information and discuss their circumstances. Some families have reported losing eight or nine relatives, according to Kashim. “In our community of Bolori II, we have many families who lost their relatives as a result of years of violence that ravaged northeastern Nigeria,” he said. Kashim said the group sometimes receives notices from the Red Cross containing names and details of missing people. These can give families leads to pursue although they do not necessarily mean a relative has been located. The association also supports children affected by the disappearances. Kashim said it was assisting about 600 orphaned children from affected families. Some attend school while others have dropped out because their relatives cannot afford to pay for their education or other basic needs. “We are now suffering because of the harsh living conditions,” he said, adding that the ICRC had distributed relief items to some families. When a missing person is a parent or breadwinner, relatives must cope with lost income while trying to provide food, shelter and schooling for children. The association’s work has consequently expanded beyond tracing missing people to helping families manage the hardships their disappearances leave behind. The search became harder for some families after devastating floods struck parts of Maiduguri in 2024. Kashim said floodwaters submerged parts of Ngarnam and destroyed photographs that families had kept to help identify missing relatives. Photographs can be vital when families try to identify people who have been rescued, displaced or found in unfamiliar communities. Without them, relatives must rely on names, physical descriptions and memories. Kashim said some families now have little beyond remembered details and surviving records to help identify their relatives. The floods added another obstacle to searches already complicated by years of conflict, displacement and uncertainty. For Kashim, finding Falmata would resolve a question that has haunted his family since 2011. His father died believing she might still return, and the family has never established whether the report of her discovery in Benin was true. Muhammad’s search for Bakura continues without the parents who once helped him look for his brother. Both families are appealing to anyone who may have information about their missing relatives. For them, finding an answer would mean more than ending a search: It would establish what happened to someone whose absence has shaped their lives for years. Kashim’s message to his sister remains a plea for a reunion that his family has waited years to see. “Falmata Mohammed, if you are alive anywhere in this world, we are the family of late Mohammed Kolo in Bolori II, Ngarnam. Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet. Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network. That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday, when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people". Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X: "Violation of those terms will result in end of service." He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately". There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.  France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus. The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029. For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death. "God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line." For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones. Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years. Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield, which is controlled by the US government, for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks. "You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations.  Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored, highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate. "Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted. Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk. While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS. "This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control." Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree. Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said. The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone. Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company. They are also about five times more expensive, she added. Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC.  She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon. Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable. Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC. Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom. But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for. That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs. Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive. Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve". No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield. But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage." Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris² is up and running in 2029. The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one. Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE. It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen. "Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites." Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid". A highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity."  So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea. "Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity." It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare." But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war." Iris² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences.  And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases. Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need "a lot of money".  Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years.  "Even if you gave me €8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained. Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare. "Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now." While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels. "In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said. A police investigation is launched after the latest round of cable theft in South Yorkshire. Some of tech's most powerful leaders are treating AI like it's alive. It could have profound consequences for our world and your own personal safety. People in the Kent village of Hunton say they have been left without answers after fibre works stop. The two leading candidates condemn recent deadly Black Sea drone strikes but differ on the war more broadly. Save Share Polls have opened in Bulgaria’s presidential election after a campaign that focused on growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping. Before Sunday’s vote, President Iliana Iotova, 61, and former caretaker Prime ⁠Minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, were leading a field of 27 candidates in the polls. ⁠The presidency is a largely ceremonial post in Bulgaria. While major policies must be approved by parliament, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, sign international treaties and appoint ambassadors. The election has also gained attention after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria that likely killed about two dozen international seafarers. The drone strikes ‌sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of Russia’s war on Ukraine, prompting Bulgaria to seek help from its allies to bolster its maritime security. The Bulgarian government has stopped short of explicitly blaming Russia for the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the outcome of the strikes “benefits the Russian Federation”. The two leading candidates for president have both condemned the strikes, but they differ on the broader war in Ukraine. Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is backed by ⁠pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He ⁠signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier. “I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe, a reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and ⁠a clear position,” he said at a rally on Thursday. Iotova, a former vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to ⁠enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many ⁠political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Radev supports Iotova, and they both have called for a diplomatic end to the war. “My opponents argue that there must be ‌a war of attrition,” Iotova said at a rally on Thursday. “The truth is, we are all the ones who are most exhausted.” While there is a broad consensus among the parties in parliament on the country’s pro-Western path, widespread pro-Russian sentiments based on traditional historical and cultural ties with Russia have divided society, particularly since the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Dobromir Zhivkov, managing director of the Market Links polling agency, said Iotova is among those who advocate that Bulgaria should take a more neutral position. “They call for an end to aid for Ukraine and a halt to arms deliveries to Ukraine. We often hear them use Kremlin rhetoric and terminology borrowed directly from Kremlin propaganda,” he told The Associated Press news agency this past week. Candidates are also addressing public fears about the steep rise in energy prices and surging inflation as many Bulgarians in rural areas struggle to make ends meet. Polls by Alpha Research suggested Iotova would win 41 percent of the vote and ‌Gyurov ‌28 percent. Voting started at 7am (05:00 GMT), and polls close at 8pm (18:00 GMT). Analysts expected none of the 27 candidates to secure the outright majority needed to win in the first round, however. Turnout must also be above 50 percent of the 6.6 million registered voters, and Sunday’s turnout is expected to be less than 40 percent, which means a likely run-off on November 1. Manchester United’s 0-3 home loss to Bournemouth has left the 20-time champions winless in eight Premier League games. Save Share Amid increasing pressure on his team and a growing threat to his own position as manager, Michael Carrick says he will do what is best for Manchester United after a 3-0 demolition by Bournemouth plunged his future into doubt. Winless in eight games in all competitions, the 20-time English champions slipped to within one point of the relegation zone after a damaging defeat at Old Trafford on Sunday.     “It’s a tough situation,” Carrick told British broadcaster Sky Sports. “What is next? I don’t know. “I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I’ve said it all along; I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility, but we’ll have to wait and see.” Asked in a post-match news conference if he expects to be sacked in the coming days, Carrick replied: “I totally understand the situation. I’m not expecting anything in particular, to be honest. I’m carrying on as normal. I love this place.” Despite a dismal run of results, the United fans largely supported the former midfielder as he made his way off the field at full-time before they turned on the club’s players. “I have mixed emotions to have that connection with the supporters in the moment we’re in. I need time to digest that,” added Carrick. “I appreciate their support but the situation is where it’s at. We haven’t been good enough.” Carrick’s decision to drop captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench and not even introduce the Portuguese international as a substitute backfired. Fernandes, last season’s Premier League player of the year, had criticised Carrick’s tactics after the 4-1 thrashing by Como on Wednesday. Carrick said before the game that his call was a “pure football” decision, but it was hard to believe Fernandes was not being punished as he was left on the bench for the entire match. “There’s always times in games when you are trying to change the course of the game and to make a difference,” said Carrick as he swerved questions on Fernandes’s absence. “Those were the decisions we made today.” Carrick was appointed on a two-year deal only in May after a successful caretaker spell in charge led United to third place in the Premier League last season. However, he has been unable to arrest the club’s steep decline since his former boss Alex Ferguson retired as manager in 2013. United were outspent by many of their rivals in the transfer market as they added just three midfielders – Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba. But Carrick said a lack of investment did not justify such a decline in results. “Last season to finish third was a really good achievement in the circumstances,” added Carrick. “We understood where that left us, what was next, what needed to be done and how we needed to improve, and where we were at as a team and as a group at that stage. “I definitely knew that we hadn’t cracked it and there was a lot of work to be done, but that doesn’t mean to say that it should have gone this way.”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

-125.56  -87.65 + 299.00  -1,149.00  -3,699.00  -125.56  -87.65  -87.65 + 299.00 + 299.00  -1,149.00  										Funds to fuel long-term growth 																															| Photo Credit: 											vkbhat 																			 The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) recently issued a circular revising the Closing Auction Session (CAS). This comes 10 weeks after the auction went live on August 3 and follows a consultation paper published in September. The circular’s message is simple: SEBI has listened to the derivatives market. From December 7, expiring index and stock derivatives will settle at the Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP) over the final 30 minutes of continuous trading, instead of the auction price. Exchanges will publish the indicative index value live during that period, and futures and options will remain open until 3:45 p.m. For derivative players and Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) bringing collateral into India to trade them, this means a steadier, more predictable settlement price. The derivatives market has had its say. Now it’s time to hear the passive investor’s voice. A passive fund doesn’t aim to beat the market; it tracks an index. Each evening, it values its portfolio at the closing price, and whenever the index is rebalanced, it trades at the close. For this kind of fund, the closing auction isn’t just another trading session — it’s where investors’ money meets the market. With settlement now moved out, CAS can become what it was designed to be: the day’s most trusted price. This is where the auction ties into Viksit Bharat. A developed India by 2047 will need a deep pool of patient domestic capital. It can come from households shifting savings from gold and fixed deposits, as well as from pension funds investing over decades. An index fund is the simplest vehicle for both. Passive funds already account for 18.6 per cent of India’s mutual fund assets, up from 9.8 per cent in 2021. The figure is 55 per cent in the United States and about 37 per cent in Japan. As India moves towards those levels, more money will need to trade at the close. This kind of patient capital steadies prices when foreign investors sell, lowers Indian companies’ cost of capital, and funds the investment growth requires. For that money to come in, the closing auction must be deep on both sides every day. Three steps can help. The first is an imbalance-only order. When index funds all need to buy at the close, the auction can become sharply one-sided. Markets such as New York and Nasdaq address this with an order that trades only against the published imbalance, and only at or better than the auction price. It cannot move the price; it can only absorb the excess. This is a natural fit for derivative players. An arbitrageur can offset a buy imbalance in the auction and hedge the position in futures, which now remain open until 3:45 p.m. SEBI’s timing change makes this order more useful. In turn, the derivatives market that SEBI has just accommodated can become the auction’s shock absorber. The second option is to build a stronger short side through the Securities Lending and Borrowing Mechanism (SLBM). An imbalance-only seller needs stock to sell, but most liquidity providers do not hold large inventories of every index stock. They therefore need to borrow shares. India’s lending market remains small compared with its cash and derivatives markets. Wider access for lenders such as mutual funds and insurers, simpler tax treatment of lending fees, and longer lending tenures would enable sellers to participate in the auction whenever buyers crowd in. The third is a fresh look at the Securities Transaction Tax (STT). At 0.1 per cent per side, it taxes turnover rather than profit. An index fund rebalancing earns nothing from the trade but pays twice. An arbitrageur, short seller or market maker who absorbs an imbalance earns a few basis points yet pays 20. When the tax exceeds the reward, liquidity providers stay away. Imbalances then widen, closing prices drift, and savers bear the cost. For a liquidity provider, if permitted, the math is even more stark. Absorbing an imbalance earns a thin margin — often just a few basis points — while a 20-basis-point round-trip STT can erase it. The provider then stays away, leaving the auction without the counterparty it needs. The logic behind STT also deserves a closer look. Introduced in 2004, it replaced the tax on long-term capital gains from listed shares, which were exempted at the same time. That exemption ended in 2018, and long-term gains are taxed again today. The original rationale for STT — a simple levy in place of a capital gains tax — therefore no longer applies to delivery trades. Investors now pay both. A significant reduction, or an exemption for trades executed in the closing auction by index funds and registered liquidity providers, would restore balance. The revenue forgone would be small, while the gains in market depth, fairer closing prices, and lower costs for savers would be substantial. Taken together, these steps would complete what the recent circular set in motion. SEBI has brought greater clarity to derivatives settlement. An imbalance-only order, a deeper lending market, and lighter STT would give passive investors a deeper close. The closing price is the one price shared by every investor in India. As passive money grows, it will carry the savings of a nation aiming to become developed by 2047. It deserves an auction designed for that future. Few brands are as synonymous with lightweight form factor and comfort as that of Crocs, and just after the biggest box office sensation of the year, it made yet another killer crossover with an iconic brand. Spider-Man has featured on every branded piece of merchandise imaginable, with even Crocs having had previous designs featuring everybody's favorite wall-crawler. Now, channeling the classics with particular focus on the red suit portions with black web-shaped accents, Crocs released their Spider-Man Neo Classic Clogs back in August 2026. With pairs available either for purchase now or future orders upon restocks, fans everywhere can order through the Crocs website for this latest Spider-Man merch drop. It comes in a variety of men's and women's sizes, perfect for casual lounging, enjoying the outdoors in balmy weather, or beating the heat and humidity whether indoors or at the beach. Given the approaching holiday season, it's also a reasonable idea to set up notifications early if some sizes aren't available, ahead of likely increased demand later in December. With any luck, Spider-Man fans in the family might just find themselves asking how those got under the Christmas tree. Currently priced at $74.99 for all men's and women's sizes, Crocs' Spider-Man Neo Classic Clog set is a hot item that's rather quick to sell out of stock. Given inflated prices showing up at StockX and FARFETCH for these but even more so for the previous Spider-Man collab, it's certainly reasonable to use the site's notification system to learn when more stock is available. While women's sizes range from 4-12, and men's from 2-13, as of this writing, all sizes are currently out of stock pending replenishment beyond women's 9 and men's 7. But whether on the Crocs website or elsewhere, it's certainly far from impossible to get a new pair without paying outrageous prices, if at least for now. The clogs themselves may not match the excellence of other recent branded crossovers like the Peanuts one complete with a plush liner, but instead, they ostensibly resemble the classic Crocs silhouette. However, far from being too simplistic, the neoprene textile shell over the exterior is made to resemble Spider-Man's super suit, stitched over the traditional Crocs, without attempting too radical of a redesign. Featuring fun little details like Spider-Man's face on each side of the heel straps, one's dedication to their favorite superhero will hardly be questioned when wearing a pair of these. With the continuously soaring popularity of Crocs and sustained mainstream popularity of everything from Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles to Chainsaw Man, it's unsurprising that products like these quickly become a hot commodity among dedicated fans. However, the durability of these clogs can be especially enticing with the combined value proposition of everyday comfort. They also make pretty solid seasonal gifts ahead of birthdays or holidays, so it's not a bad idea to be mindful of favorite franchises or characters among family members. TMNT just unveiled epic Crocs featuring the Turtles and Shredder, and the best part is that they're available for adults and kids! That all being said, some reviews for the Spider-Man Neo Classic Clog have noted some quicker deterioration of the stitching holding the textile coating on, so it's best to be mindful of what activities one might get into if they want these to have a chance at lasting long. Like with any product, it's fair to be swayed by the hype, but don't let that get in the way of what other buyers have experienced, including potential cancellations through the Crocs website, so be sure to consider backup options. With great power comes great responsibility, and even for Spider-Man, this can especially be true at the checkout page.  We want to hear from you. Thoughts on the Middle East, History and Religion © 2026 Informed Comment Mohammad Amin Ahmadi 10/25/2026  Tehran (Special to Informed Comment; Feature) –  Donald Trump has pointed to rising oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz as evidence that the energy crisis is easing. The figures offer some support for this view. In September, crude exports from the Middle East recovered to near pre-war levels on some days. Yet oil prices have remained high. On October 16, Brent crude reached $109.86 a barrel, its highest level since May. This gap between recovering exports and rising prices reveals a basic problem in Washington’s approach: the volume of oil moving through the strait is only one part of the energy market. More Oil but no Return to Normal Eastern crude exports reached an average of 14-16 million barrels per day on September. This rate suggest that exporters have found ways to move more oil despite the risks. But they do not mean that the market has returned to its previous condition. Some of the recovery has depended on changes in shipping routes, the use of more tankers, and transfers of oil between ships outside the strait. These arrangements help maintain exports, but they also add complexity and cost. As Reuters reported on October 5, the increase in flows has taken place alongside rising maritime risks and logistical limits. The difference matters. A barrel of oil leaving the Persian Gulf does not reach its destination at the same cost, speed, or level of reliability as before the war. The market responds to the cost and security of delivery, not simply to the number of barrels passing through the Strait. The Price of Insecurity The cost of shipping and insurance is one of the clearest signs of this problem. On October 12, oil-producing countries in the OPEC+ group warned that shipping and insurance costs had risen to more than one-third of the value of the commodities being transported. Such costs make energy trade more expensive even when physical flows recover. Tanker rates also remain unusually high. According to Reuters, rates for super tankers fell from their recent record levels but remained close to those highs. Insurance companies and shipping firms must consider what might happen during a voyage. A vessel may pass safely today, but the possibility of an attack tomorrow still affects insurance decisions, operating costs, and the willingness of companies to send ships into the region. These costs remain high even when more oil is moving. They also feed into the price paid by buyers, particularly when supplies are already tight and companies have few easy alternatives. The deeper problem is uncertainty. Oil prices reflect current supply and demand, but they are also shaped by expectations about future supply and the ability of traders and consumers to manage risk. A recent Federal Reserve analysis explains how a major supply shock changes the relationship between immediate oil prices and futures prices. When supplies become difficult to secure, buyers place greater value on having oil available now. Market liquidity can also weaken, making it harder to trade without affecting prices. This helps explain why a rise in oil flows does not bring prices down quickly. Buyers need confidence that supplies will remain available in the coming weeks and months. If they expect another disruption such as war, they may continue to compete for secure supplies and pay more to protect themselves against future shortages. Recent events reinforce these concerns. new attacks on ships near Hormuz and threats to Saudi energy infrastructure and more importantly news about coming war, have added to fears that supply could be disrupted again. The price increase cannot be explained by market psychology alone. Physical risks remain real. But those risks affect prices partly because they change what companies expect to happen next. America’s Miscalculation  Trump’s focus on oil flows treats the crisis mainly as a problem of quantity: if more oil passes through Hormuz, supply should improve and prices should fall. That logic misses the cost of restoring confidence in the energy system.  File photo, Kuwaiti oil tanker. US military: PHP Thomas Tolliver. Public Domain. Military action may protect some shipping routes or reduce an immediate threat, but it cannot guarantee that insurers will lower premiums, or market will stop worrying about another escalation. A statement that exports “have recovered” cannot replace evidence that trade is becoming safer and more predictable. The lesson is not that oil flows do not matter. They matter greatly. The problem is assuming that increased flows are enough to solve the challenge. Until confidence returns, higher exports will not bring lower oil prices—and, in turn, lower prices for diesel and other refined fuels. Trump can point to rising volumes of oil moving through the Strait, but the numbers alone cannot prevent prices from remaining high or even rising further. Oil prices are shaped not simply by how much oil reaches the market, but by what markets expect to happen next. And this is a challenge for which the United States has no solution, at least for now. In 2022, Kabir Nath had a cushy executive job at a pharmaceutical firm that developed anti-psychotic medication. Then he got a call from a scrappy upstart with a patent on a synthetic version of psilocybin — the active ingredient in magic mushrooms. It hoped to use the compound to help those with treatment-resistant depression. They wanted him to join as CEO. Nath, whose father died by suicide, bit on their second pitch. "A number of people have said to me in the last couple of years: 'You do realize what a risk that was,'" Nath told Business Insider about eventually jumping ship for what was, and still is, a drug company without FDA approval for its product. "I was probably the first really senior executive from traditional pharma to make the move to psychedelics," he added. "But, you know, it was the right thing to do." Nath's personal risk is now magnified as Compass Pathways finishes filing its final forms ahead of what could be FDA approval as soon as next year, and then a public rollout of its psilocybin pill, called COMP360. Compass has recently added 150 new hires to its payroll, expanded its marketing division, and moved into new office space in Jersey City in the hope it all works out. "The company is growing rapidly," Nath said. Though a subsidiary of Johnson and Johnson attained FDA approval with a version of ketamine for depression patients in 2019, it is by no means guaranteed that Compass, leveraging a more traditional psychedelic, will get the same approval. Should the FDA deny Compass' bid, investors would rush to dump their shares, likely sending the company into bankruptcy. The Jersey City office, which just received a new lime green paint job, would be untenable. If you ask Nath, it would also be bad news for 4 million patients with depression in the US, for whom more traditional antidepressants like SSRIs don't work. "These are people who have been suffering from depression, and nothing's really working," he said. Like other drug companies — especially those with a single product — Compass' stock has "been on quite the adventure," Nath said, as the company progressed through various human trials. When markets closed on Friday, the share price hovered around $11, up $5 from last year. In 2020, when the company went public, shares went for $17. Psilocybin's journey to the forefront of medical research didn't begin with Compass, and it hasn't exactly gone in a straight line. Few did more to publicize the drug than Timothy Leary, the Harvard professor turned acid dropout. In a speech at Harvard's Cambridge campus in 1962, he told students that taking psilocybin allows people to experience an "internal rebirth," according to the Harvard Crimson. In time, Leary would be fired from Harvard as he, along with a measurable portion of the US population, began to experiment more heavily with psychedelic drugs. Come 1966, the Grateful Dead were spiking their Kool-Aid with acid, and a definitive subculture of long-haired, psychedelic-taking hippies had emerged. Meanwhile, researchers were experimenting too. Studies involving LSD and psilocybin flourished during the 1960s before hitting a brick wall in 1970, when psilocybin was classified as a Schedule I substance, rendering possession illegal, even for research purposes. Work on the drug languished for years, until 2000, when the FDA gave scientists at Johns Hopkins University permission to conduct research on psilocybin. And more recently, psychedelics have become trendy with the tech crowd. From Burning Man to luxury retreats, experimenting with psychedelics is now common among tech founders and executives like Elon Musk and Sam Altman, who credit the drugs with quieting their nerves, boosting productivity, and allowing them to better harness their creativity. Research, too, has flourished. "There was actually a biotech boom from 2018 through to about 2022," Nath said. "In that boom, literally hundreds of psychedelic companies went public." In 2018, Compass' proprietary psilocybin formulation received breakthrough therapy designation from the FDA. A few years later, it started testing the drug on people. Nath was an executive in 2018 at Japanese pharmaceutical giant Otsuka, where he said he assembled a team to investigate whether psychedelics could become viable medicines after reading Michael Pollan's book "How to Change Your Mind," which explores the history and therapeutic potential of psychedelics. Compass isn't selling an experience analogous to a spiritual awakening at Burning Man, though. The drug-taking process for a patient enrolled in one of Compass' trials is a bit different. First, a patient has to have treatment-resistant depression, which is clinically defined as depression that two or more standard drugs have failed to treat. Then, a clinician explains the details of the process that is about to unfold. After that, they're given the psilocybin in pill form. "It's a quiet room with a couch," Nath said. "They're offered a blindfold, which most patients do actually wear." As the patient begins to trip, a playlist of music, including classical and new age, plays softly in the background. The clinician, who Nath said could be a nurse, doctor, or therapist, sits silently in the room if the patient wants to talk, and for safety reasons. Most of the time, though, there isn't any talking. "This is not psychotherapy," Nath said. "We are not directing the patient's experience." Six hours later, after some crying, laughing, and everything in between, the patient goes home. In Compass's most recent trial, results for which were published in September, just under half of participants who took the drug experienced at least a 50% reduction in depressive symptoms within six weeks of treatment. After a decade of slogging through tests, first on animals and then on humans, Compass has completed all the necessary prerequisites and is busily working to get its last papers in order. In a statement provided to Business Insider, an FDA spokesperson was noncommittal, though. "The FDA evaluates experimental medications, including psychedelic drugs like psilocybin, through a rigorous, evidence-based process designed to ensure that any approved treatment is safe and effective for the indicated use," the spokesperson said. Compass isn't the only psychedelic drug company wading through the lengthy process of trialing a drug. AtaiBeckley, another psychedelic drug company trading on the Nasdaq whose product is not yet approved by the FDA, is developing a version of DMT administered via nasal spray. It received breakthrough status in 2025, years behind Compass. For Compass, though, it could face the music as soon as the first half of next year, when it expects the FDA to render its decision. The company is already getting ready. In addition to adding 150 new hires, Nath said the company is preparing its sales force to go online and is in frequent communication with doctors and healthcare providers about operating in clinics where therapists can administer the drug to patients. Cypriots say Israeli money is moving fast and shutting them out as their government embraces Israel as a key ally. Save Share Various locations, Cyprus – This summer in Cyprus, on a road near Larnaca airport, a billboard greeted holidaymakers in Hebrew: “Israelis, enjoy! Now come back and win!” It was an election poster in the Cypriot city for Israel’s October 27 vote featuring Israel’s former army chief and leader of the opposition Yashar Party, Gadi Eisenkot.     The poster of Eisenkot, believed to be the first time a foreign politician had campaigned on billboards in Cyprus, signalled the growing number of Israelis living on and visiting the island, TV presenter and pro-Palestine activist Melanie Steliou told Al Jazeera. “Israel is only 40 minutes away by plane; they can pop over, vote, and come back within the day,” she said. Israel does not allow most citizens living abroad to vote outside the country, so campaigns court those who can fly home on polling day. The poster demonstrates how Israeli politicians see Cyprus as “just another district of Israel”, Steliou said. Israeli political influence is also being felt in Cyprus’s parliament. On October 20, six Cypriot lawmakers formed a pro-Israel caucus, launched by the advocacy group Israel Allies Foundation, The Jerusalem Post reported. Cyprus has absorbed waves of foreign buyers before. Limassol was once nicknamed “Limassolgrad” for its Russian community. Theodosis Pipis, a Cypriot historian and analyst with the think tank KEDISA, said that with Russian investment in the early 2010s, “you saw big buildings pop up” as companies moved over but “you never really saw a huge influx of buying houses, building schools, creating communities.” Waves of foreign money before had not shaped the island’s political climate or brought foreign election campaigns with it, he said. Israeli investment, by contrast, is creating “a sense of community for the future”, he explained.  Israelis made nearly 600,000 trips to Cyprus last year, more than double the 2022 figure, according to the Cyprus Statistical Service (CYSTAT). In August, nearly one in four tourists arriving on the island was Israeli, a 28.4 percent increase from 2025, according to CYSTAT, with some buying homes.  In the 12 months to September 2025, Israelis made 850 property purchases in Larnaca district, more than any other foreign nationality, according to Ministry of Interior data. Israel’s embassy in Nicosia estimates that 15,000 to 20,000 consider the island home, Cypriot news outlet Philenews reported in August. According to the last census in 2021, slightly more than 1,000 Israelis lived in or were registered in Cyprus.      Venetians, Ottomans and the British all held the island before independence in 1960. It has been divided since Turkiye’s 1974 invasion, which followed a coup backed by the military government in Athens. More recently, British retirees, Russian capital and golden-passport buyers have poured money into its property market. But the speed, scale and nature of new Israeli investments, to an island where walls are covered in pro-Palestine murals and graffiti amid the genocide in Gaza, have caught the attention of many. Investment from Israel rose more than sixfold between 2017 and 2024, to 5.1 billion euros ($5.9bn), according to the Central Bank of Cyprus, even as total foreign investment in the country fell by a quarter between 2022 and 2024 and Russian holdings, much of it money simply routed through Cypriot holding companies, shrank by more than a third. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, an associate professor in transitional justice and human rights at the University of Central Lancashire in Cyprus, told Al Jazeera that British and Lebanese buying “wasn’t something that made waves” and “came almost naturally”. The Israeli push, by contrast, “was a more sudden development”. That timing matters, Hadjigeorgiou said. Israel’s government keeps receiving “a lot of cover and a lot of support” from Nicosia at a time when Israel “is doing unspeakable things” in the Palestinian enclave, “and that makes at least a portion of the population uncomfortable.” Steliou pulled out her phone and showed one video – footage of a person who had been dining at an Israeli-owned restaurant attempting to attack protesters at a pro-Palestine march in Cyprus. Then another – an Israeli man writing expletives, drawing a sexual organ and spitting on a mural honouring Gaza’s children. Such events occur often, she said. Amid Israel’s wars on Gaza and Lebanon, locals interviewed by Al Jazeera said the presence of Israelis who had served in the military was hard to bear. “I feel my heart sink when I hear and see large groups of Israeli men here, knowing that they have served in the military and can commit genocide and then buy property,” Giorgos Kyrou, a 32-year-old artist from Limassol, said. Others blamed the government. “Our politicians are compromised,” said Ioannis Nestoras, a potter who lives in Limassol. “They are willing to hug, to embrace, to treat as friends the Israeli government … I don’t think it’s representative of the Cypriot mentality.” Outside the NYX Hotel Limassol, owned by Fattal, Israel’s largest hotel group, Steliou said Israeli investment appears centred on residential zones, including so-called “gated communities”. Politicians, estate agents, academics and residents in Cyprus use the phrase to describe clusters of Israeli-owned properties they see as closed off from the wider community. No official count exists, and owners’ nationalities are not recorded for purchases through Cypriot companies. But patterns are visible. Israeli companies have bought most of the coastline between Livadia and Pyla, near Larnaca, to build homes and hotels, the Cypriot financial news site Stockwatch reported last year. Stockwatch also reported that Israeli investors are promoting the largest organised residential development in Cyprus in Dromolaxia-Meneou, near Larnaca, with its own kindergarten, swimming pools, and private park. Other Cypriots share Steliou’s concerns. Kyrou said Israeli investments can focus on a particular area and that “sometimes it feels like the locals are being pushed out of those villages or urban centres”. As a historian, Pipis said he understood fears that Israel’s occupation of Palestine could be repeated, though he did not expect that in Cyprus. Instead, he believes a foothold in a friendly EU member state “offers a certain safety if things escalate more in the Middle East”. “You don’t buy these amounts of land preparing to create communities with schools … if you’re not planning to stay there for the long term,” he said. In Polemidia, on the edge of Limassol, the Yael Foundation is funding a “flagship Jewish school” for up to 1,500 pupils, due to open in 2027. Cyprus has many private and international schools serving foreign communities. Rabbi Yehoshua Smukler, who leads the project, has described this one as a “Zionist school”. Critics also point to a pattern of building first and seeking permission later. In February 2025, Cyprus’s Ministry of Education said that no application had been submitted for the school, and as late as October that year, the Ministry of Finance said the application was still being finalised, the Cypriot daily Kathimerini reported. Polemidia’s municipality, which complained it was not consulted, had itself been refused permission to build a sport centre on the same plot, the newspaper said. The ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions.      In addition to schools, other infrastructure catering to Israelis has popped up. Hadassah, one of the biggest hospital groups in Israel, owned by the US group “Hadassah, The Women’s Zionist Organization of America”, opened its first European medical centre in Limassol in July. “Specific areas are being bought en masse”, Stefanos Stefanou, leader of the left-wing Cypriot AKEL Party, said in June 2025. Purchases in Larnaca and Limassol were creating gated communities “almost inaccessible to anyone other than Israeli nationals”, he said, adding that Israel is preparing a “backyard” in Cyprus. “We do not say this because of xenophobia or anti-Semitism,” he later said. Israel’s former Ambassador to Cyprus Oren Anolik hit back, saying Stefanou’s comments sought to “single out the Jewish community in Cyprus”. Hadjigeorgiou said there was likely “some exaggeration in relation to some of the examples” of closed-off areas, but that some were “very clearly gated communities”. Speaking as a lawyer, she said Cyprus’s constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights prohibit discrimination on grounds including ethnicity, nationality and religion and that a development where only Israelis can buy “is unconstitutional”. In western Cyprus, Uriel Kertesz, a businessman with Hungarian and Israeli citizenship, bought an estimated 70 to 80 percent of the abandoned village of Trozena and its surrounding farmland, which lies in a protected area. Yiannis Pazouros, a journalist at the Cypriot daily Politis who investigated the purchases and met Kertesz, said buying as an EU citizen freed him from limits on non-EU buyers. Kertesz paid double or triple the market value and pushed ahead without the permits needed in a protected area, Pazouros said. Al Jazeera cannot independently confirm this. Despite public fears that the village could be closed off, Kertesz has stayed tight-lipped about his plans, he added. Criticism of Israel is far from uncommon in Cyprus, particularly in light of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Recently, on an October evening, Mike Kroll, an Israeli-American comedian based in Tel Aviv, played at a comedy festival in Limassol. It initially caused “apprehension” because of Israel’s image, he said. He felt “fine” with people criticising Israel because he was treated with respect and had engaged in “deep discussions”. However, his reaction has not been not universal. Across Cyprus, pro-Palestinian slogans turn public spaces into expressions of solidarity. Some are more direct in their meaning: “Zionists not welcome” reads graffiti in Larnaca. In August 2025, after Israel’s Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli complained to Cypriot ministers, the Interior Ministry ordered municipalities to remove what it called hate-inciting graffiti. In Limassol, crews removed it with uncharacteristic efficiency, sometimes before 6am, Nestoras said. The mayor initially tried to protect it as political expression but was overruled, fuelling suspicion the order came from “higher-ups”. The Interior Ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. For Cypriots, Hadjigeorgiou said, the changes carry particular weight. “We are a population that has been displaced from our homes in what the government loudly and clearly describes as ethnic cleansing. And at the same time, we are allowing another group to do the same thing in the areas that the Republic of Cyprus controls.”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Former IDF Chief of Staff Dan Halutz set off controversy on Sunday when he compared rabbis to Iran's ayatollahs. His remarks drew an angry response from United Torah Judaism Chairman MK Yaakov Asher, who reminded Halutz of the controversy surrounding the sale of his stocks at the outbreak of the Second Lebanon War. In an interview on the "Moshe Fabrikant Podcast," Halutz addressed the leaders of the Haredi community, including yeshiva dean Rabbi Moshe Hillel Hirsch and the rabbis of the Shas movement, saying: "I see no difference between the ayatollahs in Iran and the rabbis in Israel." Halutz continued to compare Israel's rabbinical leadership to Iran's religious leaders: "Is Rabbi Hirsch any better because he speaks Yiddish? Are the rabbis of Shas any better? In Iran, there is no Sephardic ayatollah and Ashkenazi ayatollah. There is just one." Following the remarks, MK Yaakov Asher issued a scathing response, personally attacking Halutz and recalling his conduct during the Second Lebanon War. "Take off your shoes! A despicable man like you, who, while serving as IDF Chief of Staff, just minutes before sending soldiers into the Second Lebanon War, some of whom sadly never returned alive, was concerned at those fateful moments with nothing more than calling the bank to sell your stocks," Asher wrote. Asher concluded his response with another attack, invoking a comparison to Iran: "Such depravity may not even exist at the headquarters of Iran's Revolutionary Guards."
