The deputy secretary-general of the UN’s ICT agency tells Al Jazeera that unequal access to AI means poorer nations may be left behind. Save Share Doha, Qatar – Artificial intelligence (AI) risks widening the gap between rich and poor countries, potentially deepening existing social and economic inequalities, a senior United Nations official has warned. Developing countries face significant barriers to benefitting from the AI revolution, Tomas Lamanauskas, the deputy secretary-general of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a UN agency focused on information and communication technologies, told Al Jazeera. “There is a risk … I think the AI divide is really the big concern because it’s really not just about the digital divide,” Lamanauskas said on the sidelines of the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Forum in Doha, Qatar on Sunday. “AI has the huge potential of powering health, education, public services, industries, agriculture, trade. So a great divide could really mean an opportunity divide, and really could deepen the socioeconomic divide,” he said. “So that’s really the worrying part.”      Lamanauskas said the disparities are already evident in digital infrastructure, citing the examples of Africa and Latin America, which together account for just 3.3 percent of global data centre capacity. “So you clearly see still a rather big infrastructure divide,” he said, adding that 2.2 billion people worldwide remain without internet access. In a December 2025 report, the UN Development Programme (UNDP) cautioned that AI could trigger a new era of inequality between nations, reversing decades of progress in narrowing economic disparities between nations. The UNDP warned that countries with unreliable power, limited connectivity, and a lack of technological skills risk missing out on the economic gains of AI. Bridging the digital infrastructure gap would require an estimated $2.8 trillion in investment by 2030, UN official Lamanauskas said. The divide between nations is also evident in the adoption of AI, he added. While approximately 29 percent of working-age people in developed countries use generative AI, that figure drops to 16 percent in developing nations. “This actually affects your ability to be productive and to be part of job-market opportunities,” Lamanauskas said. Lamanauskas acknowledged growing concerns about AI-driven job losses, citing estimates that the technology could displace 90 million jobs, but also create 170 million new ones. However, he warned that even if there is a “net positive impact”, many people will personally experience disruption, as an estimated 40 percent of workplace skills could change by 2030. He also pointed to language inequalities, revealing that only seven percent of African languages are represented in AI translation tools, limiting access for millions of potential users. According to the 2026 International AI Safety Report released in February, about one billion people use AI for a variety of tasks, including seeking guidance on medical health and writing.      While no concrete data exists, the report estimated that about 60 percent of jobs in advanced economies and 40 percent in emerging economies could be exposed to AI-related impacts. “The fears are real,” said Fazl Barez, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford specialising in AI safety and governance. However, he cautioned that it was important to distinguish between AI “automating tasks and replacing entire jobs”. “What are the types of jobs that could be lost? Those involving routine cognitive work are particularly exposed, but the scale remains uncertain,” Barez told Al Jazeera. “AI-driven automation threatens to erode government tax bases, lower living standards, and disempower citizens.” Despite concerns around the AI revolution, Lamanauskas said he did not believe there was a “possibility just to stop AI” or halt its rapid advancement. “AI is here to stay, and AI is here to transform our lives,” he said, noting that 104 countries now have AI strategies, compared with just four a decade ago. “AI is not a technology that can be controlled by one person or organisation or one company,” the UN official added. Nevertheless, he called for greater investment in digital infrastructure, education and regulation to ensure developing countries can participate in helping shape the technology. “The way forward is really to invest to make sure that the AI benefits everyone, to recognise and acknowledge the fears and anxieties that people feel,” he said. Bangladesh is expected to surpass India’s per capita GDP this year, but the complete economic picture is a mix of success stories and new challenges. Save Share Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product (GDP) is projected to be higher than that of Asia’s third largest economy, India, this year, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF). GDP is a measure of all goods and services produced within a country during a specific period. India’s GDP is nearly eight times larger than Bangladesh’s. But its neighbour’s per capita GDP, which is GDP divided by the total population, is expected to surpass that of India, the world’s most populous nation.     The projected 2026 per capita GDP of Bangladesh, home to about 175 million people, is $2,886, compared with $2,749 in India as Dhaka emerges as one of South Asia’s notable economic success stories over the past two decades. Bangladesh’s economy is currently larger than that of Pakistan, from which Dhaka seceded in 1971. Experts link the rise to the country’s $38bn garment industry, remittances and growing participation of women in the workforce. But high inflation and slowing growth are now putting that progress under pressure. Meanwhile, the Indian economy is expected to grow by 7 percent this year, compared with 3.6 percent in Bangladesh. So how should one read these numbers, and what do they really mean for millions of people living in these countries? The IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook report underscores differences in how the Indian and Bangladeshi economies are reacting to inflation and the economic pressures caused by two major wars that have jolted energy markets. Bangladesh is expected to have a GDP of $506.4bn in 2026, compared with India’s $4.15 trillion. But its lead in GDP per capita reverses when adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP), which accounts for differences in local prices. On this measure, India is projected to have a GDP per capita at $12,998, compared with Bangladesh’s $10,884. PPP is an economic metric that represents what money can actually buy in different countries after adjusting for the cost of living. The figures mean that Indians have a higher buying capacity than Bangladeshis. The IMF projected India’s average consumer-price inflation at 5 percent, compared with 8.7 percent in Bangladesh, pointing to greater cost-of-living pressures in Dhaka. India is relatively wealthier than Bangladesh and is home to a big industrial base, including its significant technology sector. India’s economy is expected to grow by 7 percent in 2026, nearly twice Bangladesh’s 3.6 percent rate. For context, the average per capita GDP in developing economies is about $7,746 – and the global average is about $15,889 – against Bangladesh’s $2,886 and India’s $2,749. In the next year, the IMF report projected that Bangladesh’s per capita GDP would reach $3,219, still higher than India’s $3,036 – a difference, according to the estimates, that should continue marginally in 2028. In 2029, based on current growth forecasts, India’s per capita GDP of $3,661 would top Bangladesh’s $3,334, according to the IMF. Experts noted that Bangladesh is facing a weaker near-term growth outlook, even as its projected GDP per capita edges above India’s. But GDP per capita alone does not paint a complete economic picture because it conceals inequalities in income and wealth distribution. The dollar-denominated figure also changes with the exchange rate, which means that a change in a currency’s value can alter the relative numbers without a change in economic output. In brief, the growth in Bangladesh’s economy in the past two decades has focused on export-oriented manufacturing, particularly its ready-made garment industry, which has been a major source of export earnings and employment, in addition to remittances from Bangladeshis working abroad. Meanwhile, India has a diversified economy, with services playing a major role alongside manufacturing and agriculture. Its domestic market, technology and business services, industrial base and consumer demand provide multiple sources of economic activity. In both countries, however, economic growth over the past decade has been unequal with increasing concentration in wealthier households.      To some extent, yes, analysts said while expressing caution about unequal growth. Santosh Mehrotra, an Indian economist, told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh’s economy has shown consistent economic growth of 6 percent per annum alongside a long-term decline in population growth. The country has also seen its manufacturing contribution to gross value added shoot up from 16.6 percent in 2014 to 22 percent in 2025, Mehrotra said. On the other hand, World Bank data showed India’s manufacturing value added falling from 15.1 percent of GDP in 2014 to 13.5 percent in 2024. “That’s a positive side of export-oriented manufacturing growth that Bangladesh is getting right,” he said. However, the global energy shock from the United States-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, has jolted Bangladesh. Bangladesh imports 95 percent of its oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and much of these imports comes from the Middle East. The ready‑made garment industry, which accounts for more than 80 percent of Bangladesh’s export earnings, has also been hit as its shipment routes via the Red Sea and the Middle East have been disrupted. Not so long ago, you could have compared Hyundai (and sister company Kia) to the numerous Chinese newcomers currently wreaking havoc on the new car market. The pair did to the legacy automakers what the Chinese are doing now, in so much as they undercut prices with exceptional value propositions. How times have changed, as both Korean marques now offer luxurious electric vehicles that cost upwards of £70,000 / $70,000 / AU$130,000 and are now synonymous with quality, innovation and cutting-edge design. However, these companies also now find themselves fending off cut-price competition from the Far East. Not one to back down, Hyundai is ploughing on with its plans to be one of the leading electric vehicle manufacturers in the world, promising to launch or update 100 models by the year 2030.      Spearheading that campaign is the new Ioniq 3 — a fully electric compact hatchback that Hyundai says is designed to make electrified mobility intuitive, comfortable and relevant for everyday European needs. To do this, it is offering highly competitive all-electric range, punchy performance and distinctive looks in a package that can easily be threaded through busy city streets and parked in typically tight urban spaces. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. But above all this is the exceptional value proposition. In the UK, the Hyundai Ioniq 3 starts at £18,495 after the full £3,750 Electric Car Grant (that's around $25,000 / AU$35,000), slotting it in among some of the most affordable EVs on the market today, without the tech and space compromises of something like the super cheap Dacia Spring, Honda Super-N or Leapmotor T03.      It might seem odd that one of Hyundai’s cheapest vehicles is also the first to sport Hyundai’s all-new Pleos infotainment system, but the technological update has helped keep costs down. Gone is the sweeping (and more expensive) multi-screen array found in other models, such as the Ioniq 5, and in its place is either a 12.9-inch or 14.6-inch central touchscreen (depending on the trim level) that is based on the now ubiquitous Android Automotive Operating System. Zero points for guessing which company Pleos clearly drew a huge amount of inspiration from, as the graphical layout is almost identical to a Tesla, complete with the ability to adjust the on-screen set-up with a few intuitive swipes.      Zero points for guessing which company Pleos clearly drew a huge amount of inspiration from There’s a graphical representation of the car on the left of the screen that can open the trunk and windows (like Tesla), navigation to the right (like Tesla) and a read-out for current speed in the corner closest to the driver (you guessed it, just like Tesla). Homework copying aside, Pleos isn’t as handsome as other Hyundai set-ups, as it feels a little ‘bolted on’ to the dash. But it all works seamlessly, is very fast to respond and is an improvement in so much as it offers much more detailed connected navigation with EV route planning, over-the-air software updates and access to the Pleos App Market, which will grow as the weeks pass. Weirdly, Hyundai has also opted to offer a second digital driver display, which sits behind the steering wheel, as an optional extra. Some corners of the internet lost their minds over this, forgetting that Tesla has relied solely on its central infotainment display for years.      So, if you prefer your speed read-outs in a position where you don’t have to take your eyes off the road, it could be worth ticking that option box. Hyundai also introduces Gleo AI with the new infotainment system, an AI-powered voice assistant integrated into Pleos Connect. It uses natural-language commands to control selected vehicle functions, access information and interact with connected services. During testing, it worked very well, able to make the cabin warmer via chatty conversation and even interact with third-party apps, such as Spotify. There’s also the option of Hyundai Digital Key 2, which allows compatible smartphones and wearable devices to lock, unlock and start the car without a physical key, while a dedicated app provides remote access to vehicle information and selected functions through a smartphone. Despite the price, customers aren’t getting short-changed on the technology front and here, it feels like Hyundai has poured hours of dev work into the Ioniq 3 to make sure it’s all intuitive and easy to figure out… which can’t be said for many cut-price Chinese rivals.      Hyundai’s decision to combine its ‘Art of Steel’ design language with what the company calls an ‘Aero Hatch’ silhouette is likely to raise eyebrows and cause some debate over whether or not it actually works, but this is a car that demands attention whichever side of the argument you sit on. The shape pairs a low front end with a roofline designed to maximize headroom for front and rear passengers before tapering toward the rear spoiler. Hyundai said it targeted a drag coefficient of approximately 0.263 in order to boost EV efficiency, while the company’s signature pixel lighting and four central dots referencing the letter ‘H’ in Morse code give the car a distinctive visual identity when it’s dark.      Divisive exterior design aside, there’s plenty of room inside the car. The ‘Furnished Space’ approach of the concept has taken a bit of a backseat, but it’s a very minimalist space with a flat floor that’s intended to maximize passenger roominess, with Hyundai claiming the five-seat cabin can comfortably accommodate three adults in the rear — although it will be a squeeze. Customers can stash a total of 441 liters of stuff in the back, which is split between a 322-liter trunk and an integrated 119-liter “Megabox”, which is essentially a large space underneath the trunk floor. Having seen most of the variations Hyundai offers, the N-Line cars, with their larger wheels and more pronounced rear spoiler, certainly look the best. It’s no hot hatch, but ‘Aero Hatch’ wears the rear wing and diffuser with more confidence, making it look less awkward than base cars.      Navigating Hyundai’s various trim levels is a little confusing, especially given that the cheaper, shorter-range versions are actually faster — which you can't specify in the racier N-Line guise. All cars ride on Hyundai’s latest K3 Platform with a 400-volt electrical architecture, allowing for 10 to 80% top-ups in approximately 29 minutes using a DC fast charger. The Standard Range model uses a 42.2 kWh battery, while the Long Range version gets a 61 kWh unit. Both feature a front-mounted electric motor and front-wheel drive, with the Standard Range producing 107.8 kW (147 hp) and the Long Range delivering 99.5 kW (135 hp). It feels like the wrong way around, but it’s very difficult to discern the additional 12 hp from behind the wheel anyway.      The ‘Furnished Space’ approach of the concept has taken a bit of a backseat Hyundai quotes WLTP ranges of over 344km (around 214 miles) for the Standard Range and over 497km (around 310 miles) for the Long Range, which feels about right given the sort of efficiencies we were experiencing during our test drives. Across the often broken road surfaces just outside of Istanbul, Turkey, the Ioniq 3 leaned on its smart regenerative braking functionality to top up the batteries on descents and generally make the most out of a charge. I clocked around 4.2 miles per kWh during my test. With that in mind, expect to return around 250 miles from the longer-range versions and around 200+ miles from the Standard variant under typical driving conditions. Acceleration is brisk across the board and this is definitely a car that has been tuned for quick city sprints, rather than long motorway stretches.      During these, there’s a fair amount of wind noise and the Ioniq 3 felt out of its depth keeping up with Turkey’s circa-90 mph speed limits. But under normal (read slower) driving conditions, it feels much more mature than its budget price tag would suggest. The cabin is neatly laid out and the soft-touch fabrics adorning most surfaces elevate it to a point that Hyundai could easily charge more. Above all else, it’s very difficult not to keep returning to the price, because the Ioniq 3 feels like an extremely accomplished EV that will happily rival the likes of the Renault 5 E-Tech and the VW ID 3, while undercutting sister company Kia’s EV2 by a considerable amount. As a retort to the waves of cheaper Chinese rivals, it’s a formidable proposition with great in-car tech, a sweet drive, excellent range and a premium-felling interior. In fact, when you consider the price, it has to be one of the most well-rounded affordable EVs currently on sale. Week 7 of the college football season was great, but so was Week 8. Another week full of upsets and close finishes. After stunning Notre Dame last weekend, BYU hit the road as the new No. 2 ranked team in the country, but the Cougars fell to UCF in overtime as Bear Bachmeier’s pass couldn’t find his target.  But that wasn’t the only big upset. Texas Tech stumbled for the first time this season as the Red Raiders traveled to Cincinnati to take on the Bearcats. Ole Miss fell to Texas and Iowa lost on the road to Minnesota. Both USC and Tennessee lost their road games to Wisconsin and South Carolina, respectively.  Following another big day of college football, here is our latest stock report.  MORE: Malachi Toney broke his own Miami football record on Saturday It was hard to live up to Week 7, but Week 8 certainly didn’t disappoint. The NFL has a saying of ‘On any given Sunday’, but college football is starting to take on that slogan. Parity is at an all-time high in the sport and each week there are multiple upsets.  On Saturday, there were three top-10 teams upset. After the top 10, Tennessee went down to South Carolina, Minnesota beat Iowa in a low-scoring Big Ten game, and Wisconsin took down USC. And if you like overtime games both the Indiana vs. Michigan and BYU vs. UCF games went into overtime to add additional excitement.  Some weeks might not look super appealing on paper, but once the chaos begins, it’s hard to look away.  Entering Saturday, there were three Big 12 teams ranking inside the top 10 and the conference was starting to get some respect. But, as predicted, there were two major upsets. After upsetting Notre Dame last weekend, BYU lost to UCF in overtime. Texas Tech went on the road and was handled by Cincinnati, a team that lost two games in a row.  Utah was the lone undefeated Big 12 team to win its game. The Utes had a low-scoring affair against Houston. The Cougars had chances to upset Utah, but Devon Dampier and Co. pulled it out to remain at the top of the conference.  BYU will play Utah this season, but Texas Tech misses both the Cougars and Utes. That’s good for the Red Raiders, but Texas Tech could very easily have multiple losses this season. This isn’t the same Red Raiders’ defense as last season, and the Big 12 might pick each other apart too much to get more than one team into the playoff.  Speaking of parity, it’s at an all-time high in the Big Ten. UCLA won once again on Saturday, over Michigan State, to remain unbeaten on the season. Ohio State still hasn’t lost a conference game, but it’s wide open past those two teams.  Northwestern continues to win games. And then there are Minnesota and Wisconsin, who pulled off home upsets. The Gophers weren’t expected to compete with Iowa, but Minnesota won 13-10. Then the Badgers took down the explosive Trojans’ offense, 24-7.  The typical stout Big Ten teams like Oregon, Michigan, and Penn State are all bad. It’s a new era of college football and the blue bloods are figuring that out  After suffering the 41-27 loss to Oregon a few weeks back, USC has just been getting by. The Trojans won one-score games over both Washington and Penn State, but USC met its match on Saturday.  Wisconsin’s offense scored seven points two weeks ago against UCLA, and the Badgers’ offense was lackluster once again. Colton Joseph threw for a meager 58 yards and Wisconsin ran for 142 yards. But it didn’t matter.  USC’s offense was dismal and Jayden Maiava threw two interceptions. Lincoln Riley lost another game he should’ve won and the pressure is really going to start mounting. USC still has to play Ohio State, Indiana, and UCLA this season. It’s not impossible that the Trojans lose all three games. They’ve yet to make the CFP under Riley and that’s unacceptable.  After losing two games in a row, Texas’ SEC and CFP lives were on the line. With so many upsets each week, there could be a few 9-3 teams making the playoff in 2026, but Texas didn’t want three losses this early. And the Longhorns got out to a 24-3 lead over Ole Miss. But in typical Texas style, the Longhorns let the Rebels back into the game. Ole Miss kicked a field goal with 1:22 left in the game to pull within seven. The Rebels then recovered the onside kick to give Trinidad Chambliss a chance to tie the game, but Texas intercepted his Hail Mary attempt.  Arch Manning didn’t play well. He threw two interceptions, but Texas’ defense made enough plays to allow the Longhorns to win the game. The SEC keeps picking each other off, but the Longhorns remain alive.  In-season firings are taking place and North Carolina State made the second one this week. Mike Locksley was fired at Maryland, and now Dave Doeren lost his job at NC State. The Wolfpack fired Doeren after a 3-4 start to the 2026 season. NC State had some big expectations this year in an open ACC, especially with CJ Bailey returning at quarterback.  Doeren has coached NC State since 2013 and has a 98-74 record. With the federal budget deficit at $2 trillion and debt-interest costs topping $1 trillion a year, it may be tempting to look for extra cash under the sofa cushions.  Urgency has grown in recent months as Treasury yields have soared to the highest levels in more than 20 years, putting more pressure on interest expenses. The Treasury Department has tried some unconventional measures recently to take the heat off yields, including buybacks of more long-dated debt and its intervention to prop up the yen that let Japan avoid selling its Treasuries. Given such surprises, speculation has grown around even more far-out tactics. One idea that comes up from time to time is for the Treasury Department to price its immense gold holdings at market rates.  The U.S. has the world’s largest gold reserves, which total about 261.5 million ounces, or more than double what No. 2 holder Germany has. But the U.S. hoard’s official price was set by Congress in 1973 at $42.22 per ounce, and it hasn’t changed since.  That means all that gold is only on the books for just over $11 billion. But if it was valued at gold’s current price of around $4,000 per ounce, it would be worth $1 trillion. Comments by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last year that the government would “monetize the asset side of the U.S. balance sheet” and create a sovereign wealth fund fueled talk that it could include repricing gold, though the administration later said it’s not under serious consideration. But scrutiny into U.S. gold reserves keeps popping up. For instance, a recent bill in Congress to establish a strategic bitcoin reserve proposed repricing U.S. gold holdings. And last year, President Donald Trump questioned whether the gold held in the Fort Knox U.S. Army base was actually there. (The Treasury’s gold is also held in Denver, the New York Fed, and West Point, NY.) In July of this year, Bessent reignited theories about gold. He said the cache at Fort Knox is all “present and accounted for” — then casually added “the U.S. has the largest pile of gold in the world, over a trillion dollars at current market value.”  Jurrien Timmer, director of global macro at Fidelity Investments, started thinking about “what other tricks the Treasury Department might have up its sleeve to try to bring down the cost of funding.” In a post on X on Friday, he tackled the “old meme” of the Treasury repricing its gold to market rates, theoretically giving the federal government another $1 trillion to spend without having to issue more debt. “Far-fetched? Of course, but these days I have learned to never be shocked by anything anymore. Notwithstanding that an action like this would require congressional approval, my guess is that if the Treasury were attempt do this, it would backfire in a big way,” Timmer warned. For one thing, the U.S. dollar would take a hit, he predicted, presumably as a sudden influx of $1 trillion would stoke more inflation, which is already heating up. Timmer also cautioned that the “term premium” in Treasury yields would rise even higher. Rates have shot up in recent months for a combination of reasons, including expectations for Fed rate hikes, robust economic growth, and persistent inflation. But the so-called term premium, or the extra return investors demand to cover the risk of holding debt over the long term, has also climbed. Such risks could range from more geopolitical turmoil to a fiscal crisis or an economic downturn. While it may seem unlikely in the U.S., other countries have revalued their gold reserves over the last 30 years. A note from a Federal Reserve economist last August pointed out that Germany, Italy, Lebanon, Curacao and St. Maarten, and South Africa have done so.  In Italy and Curacao and St. Maarten, their central banks used the proceeds. In South Africa, Lebanon, and Germany, their central governments reaped the windfall. But when it comes to reducing a country’s debt burden, gold revaluation isn’t enough, the Fed note added. That’s as gross U.S. debt has soared to $40 trillion, and no end in sight to $2 trillion annual budget deficits. “Central governments have drawn on revaluation proceeds to retire existing debts, often in exceptional fiscal circumstances,” the Fed note added. “While reducing the debt stock using revaluation proceeds improves the fiscal situation at the margin, drawing on revaluation proceeds may not address larger structural challenges.”   Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune, where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing. © 2026 Fortune Media IP Limited. Sometime in the late 1980s, Doris Ruffin’s decrepit market-rate apartment in Harlem collapsed. With nowhere else to go, she took her young nephew, Prince, to a city shelter. For months they lived there, occupying a kind of limbo, protected from the elements but never really settled. Ruffin is not one for big emotional displays, but when a social worker helped her find a place at the Elliott-Chelsea Houses, a public housing complex on the West Side of Manhattan, she was overcome with relief. “I felt like the heavens had opened up,” she said. The apartment was nothing fancy, but it was a home. And at 30 percent of her income—the policy for public housing—the price was right. “Now I had a stable, affordable place to live.” Ruffin has been at Elliott-Chelsea for more than 30 years. The apartment’s two bedrooms allowed her to raise Prince, who liked keeping small pets and fixing electronics, until he was a teenager. She often worked two security jobs at a time to make ends meet. Eventually, she earned a master’s degree in speech therapy. By the late 2010s, Ruffin was making a decent salary and paying a little over $1,500 a month, still a manageable sum in a neighborhood that she had watched transform as artists and luxury retailers crept in, followed by the lush tourist trap of the High Line park, the gleaming towers of Hudson Yards, and the soaring rents that came along with them. Public housing continued to support Ruffin in 2019, when a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, a cancer of the blood plasma, forced her to retire. The treatment damaged her kidneys and she went on dialysis, withdrawing her pension to cover her mounting medical expenses. By then, her apartment had mold problems, and the New York City Housing Authority, racked by decades of federal disinvestment, was slow to remediate. Her property manager helped place her in a seniors-only building where the units were clean and large enough to fit her new rolling walker. Friends from the community visited to check on her. Together, they would take walks at the park nearby or watch Knicks games on TV. From her window, she could look out over a rippling canopy of green and the Empire State Building rising above it. One day in 2024, Doris Ruffin returned to her apartment after a long hospital stay to find a notice from NYCHA taped to her door: She would be relocated. The housing authority—working with Related Companies, the mega-developer of Hudson Yards, and its spin-off firm Essence Development—intended to demolish and rebuild her home, along with the whole of Elliott-Chelsea and the nearby Fulton Houses. Ruffin’s building would be among the first leveled. Staff “relocation specialists” would help the 67-year-old move into a different unit in the complex. In a few years’ time, she would be placed into a brand-new building packed with modern amenities like fitness centers and central AC. Ruffin was unmoved by this pledge. “I was in disbelief,” she said. Sure, the elevators needed an overhaul, and the plumbing clearly deserved repairs. But why did these problems require a teardown? “I was in disbelief,” she said. Sure, the elevators needed an overhaul, and the plumbing clearly deserved repairs. But why did these problems require a teardown? The plan to transform Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea falls under a federal scheme that allows local agencies to convert developments out of the public housing system and bring on private real estate companies that can finance their rehab or reconstruction. Often, these partners are big corporate landlords that are more than happy to take over managing the homes—and collecting the government-guaranteed rent that they provide. As Congress has withdrawn funding from public housing, many cities have used the program to turn their entire portfolios over to private managers. This might be fine if the companies consistently delivered big upgrades. But the program does not exactly have a stellar track record. A 2018 report from the Government Accountability Office found that large percentages of tenants in converted developments nationwide reported poor renovation quality and nonresponsive management, and a 2022 assessment from Human Rights Watch warned that, in New York City, it has “negatively impacted the right to housing of low-income residents by leading to a reduction in oversight.” That neglect has caused a range of serious problems for tenants, from increased evictions to poor living conditions. NYCHA, however, has bulldozed ahead. So far, the agency has converted around a quarter of its public housing stock, and its plan for Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea is especially aggressive. Under a $1.9 billion proposal, Related and Essence would conduct the first demolition under the program, razing all 18 buildings of the complexes and replacing them with six high-rise towers for public housing residents. The developers would erect thousands of new mixed-income apartments on the remainder of the land, some of the most valuable on the planet. Tenants have described a planning process riddled with deceptions and disregard for their input. But with the housing authority staring down roughly $78 billion in backlogged maintenance over the next 20 years, officials have said that the cash flow from this conversion is one of the few ways to give the aging apartments the repairs they need. The agency views the project as a model for other developments, according to NYCHA’s chief executive, Lisa Bova-Hiatt. None of this smelled right to Ruffin. “These developers are just being greedy,” she said, her eyes growing big. “They don’t care about the people and how it’s affecting them.” When she viewed the temporary apartment that NYCHA had reserved for her, she found small, narrow rooms that were impossible to navigate with her walker. Ruffin decided that she was staying put. In her 14-floor building, she is one of 24 holdouts, as of late September. Six other families have refused to move out of a mid-rise in Fulton, the first marked for demolition in that complex. Together with tenants across their community, they are fighting in street rallies and in court against a plan that they view as a land grab. “This is what we’re used to, this is our environment,” Ruffin said. “If you take that away, you’re taking everything away from us.” In picking this fight, Ruffin and her neighbors are battling a political behemoth. Not only do the housing authority and its real estate partners favor the plan. New York City’s new democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani, who campaigned on holding corporate landlords accountable, seems eager to turn public housing over to private companies if it means a quick fix for troubled infrastructure. And in Washington, bipartisan members of Congress recently authorized a vast expansion of such conversions nationwide, a continuation of a decades-long retreat from direct control of public goods. As the country unwinds the social gains of the twentieth century, what remains for public housing tenants? Public housing began as a grand social democratic experiment. Born from the economic depths of the Great Depression, the Housing Act of 1937 charged government with creating affordable rentals for working Americans, a stout brick bulwark against the slums of the for-profit housing market. The idea was not without opposition. Politicians on both sides of the aisle smeared it as socialist, and real estate groups decried it as a threat to their livelihood. In the end, the program, known formally as Section 9 of the law, was a compromise, ensuring that public housing would be built to minimum standards and reserved for the poorest citizens, so as not to compete with the private market. Still, into the postwar era, its segregated garden apartments and squat brick townhouses enjoyed a foothold in urban life. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, in his 1944 State of the Union address, nodded to the program when he declared “the right of every family to a decent home.” Over the decades, however, that sunny New Deal vision has clouded. In the midcentury, cities struggled as white residents fled for the suburbs, lured by incentives denied to families of color. Public housing became the high-rise terrain of a Black urban underclass. Politicians and the media blamed the projects for rising crime and poverty, despite the vibrant communities millions still found there. Beginning in the 1970s, notorious superblocks, like St. Louis’s Pruitt-Igoe and Chicago’s Cabrini-Green, served as justification for Congress to drastically defund the Department of Housing and Urban Development. Local agencies spiraled into dysfunction; much public housing was allowed to deteriorate. In 1995, President Bill Clinton promised to “end public housing as we know it,” a bid for bipartisan agreement. “Most public housing worked pretty well,” said Edward Goetz, a professor of urban planning at the University of Minnesota and the author of New Deal Ruins: Race, Economic Justice, and Public Housing Policy. “Yet we embarked on this large-scale effort to eliminate it.” Plumes of debris rose from Chicago to Atlanta to New Orleans, where agencies took federal grants to sell off or detonate their public housing, as white, affluent families streamed back to urban centers. On the grounds, developers built mixed-income rentals, but most public housing was never replaced. Even at this stage, politicized tenants understood these “transformations” as a land grab. Some were given government-issued vouchers to rent from landlords in the private market; many were pushed out of the system altogether when they were rescreened for eligibility. Thousands of families were scattered into other poor and segregated pockets of the urban landscape. Nationally, the number of public housing units has fallen from 1.4 million at the program’s postwar peak to 860,000 today, even as the waiting lists in big cities reach the hundreds of thousands. Into this smoky air of decline, HUD launched a new plan for public housing transformation. Adopted in 2012, the Rental Assistance Demonstration, or RAD, is a classic Obama-era public-private partnership—much like the deals that cities strike with companies to manage everything from utilities to hospitals. Under the program, local agencies can convert public housing into what’s called project-based Section 8 housing, a different form of low-income rental that provides roughly double the funding stream. The public still owns the land, while the private partner leases it for 99 years and takes a 50 percent stake in the venture. The idea is that these companies can borrow private capital and access tax credits to finance repairs in ways that housing agencies can’t. Unlike the diabolical demolition schemes of the 1990s and 2000s, the program stipulates one-for-one replacement of public housing units and guarantees tenants the right to return, with the same rent and without rescreening. For struggling housing authorities, the advent of the program was something of a stunner, said Paul Williams, a housing policy analyst who serves as executive director of the Center for Public Enterprise. He described it as a “life hack” for the agencies. Historically, New York City has preserved its public housing. NYCHA is the largest housing authority in the country. It’s responsible for some 400,000 tenants across 335 developments, the equivalent of a midsize city. And while the agency has had its share of dysfunction, it was long the well-run exception to the bad big-city systems—“public housing that worked,” as its most prominent historian once described it. But decades of austerity have caught up to NYCHA. As with virtually all housing authorities, its apartments literally cost more to run than it receives in rent and subsidies combined. In 2018, NYCHA was forced into a federal consent decree requiring agencywide reforms and repairs to dangerous conditions like lead, mold, and broken elevators. It’s easy to see the bind that housing authorities like NYCHA face, and why many cities are racing to partner with deep-pocketed landlords. “We are limited in the tools that we have to try to reverse the decades and decades of federal disinvestment,” Bova-Hiatt said. From the outset, however, RAD had problems. Certainly, the program attracted billions in investment, and there were complexes where it resulted in serviceable rehabs. But introducing corporate landlords with a profit motive meant completely changing the incentive structure of running these homes. Plenty imported their habitual cost-cutting practices. “When you bring in these new companies, some of them have very checkered histories,” said Iziah Thompson, a senior policy analyst at the Community Service Society of New York. “Some of them are companies that the tenant movement has been fighting as ‘slumlords’ in the low-income housing space for years.” For these reasons, many advocates have come to see the program not as a “life hack” but as another spasm in the death throes of public housing. In January, Doris Ruffin held onto her walker as she spoke into a cluster of local news mics at the entrance of the Hudson Guild, Elliott-Chelsea’s community center. Dressed in layers against the cold, she admonished NYCHA for harassing her. Flanking Ruffin were residents of the complexes, supporters from the Chelsea neighborhood, the Democratic district leader, a former state senator, and members of local left-wing organizations. After the seniors refused to leave, NYCHA began putting heat on them, they allege. Agency staff knocked on their doors day and night. Notices arrived threatening lease termination for unspecified rule violations. Many of the seniors are ill, disabled, or speak limited English. NYCHA, for its part, has said that all these measures were taken in the spirit of providing tenants with accurate information about the plan and the terms of their lease. In 2025, the housing authority sued 16 residents, including Ruffin, in hopes that a judge would have them removed; the judge declined, and the agency withdrew its request. But some tenants were intimidated by these tactics. “It is not right,” Ruffin said to the crowd. “It is not ethical.” Standing at Ruffin’s side was Renee Keitt, looking on protectively from behind thick-rimmed black eyeglasses. An urban farmer and community organizer, Keitt grew up in Elliott-Chelsea. Her mother lives in the complex. Her grandmother died there. In early 2025, Keitt became the resident association president by running an insurgent campaign against NYCHA’s redevelopment scheme, unseating a longtime incumbent who supported the plan. Since then, she has served as the de facto leader of the opposition. “Nobody has asked us,” Keitt said during her turn at the mics. “We demand that you start listening.” How the process of repairing Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea became a crucible for the fate of public housing in New York is a long and complicated story. But as Keitt indicates, it begins and ends with tenants feeling that their wishes are being ignored, a familiar experience for people of color across the United States whose government-run homes a city has decided to tear down in order to make room for the more affluent. Back in 2019, officials gave up on an initial plan to demolish two Fulton buildings and replace them with mixed-income towers when residents revolted. Chastened, the mayor’s office launched a working group process, where tenant representatives, community board members, and officials hashed out the gritty details of repairing both complexes under the local RAD variant (known as Permanent Affordability Commitment Together, or PACT). There were asbestos issues to consider, as well as leaks, mold, outdated elevators, and faulty heat and hot water. A delicate compromise was reached, with tenants agreeing to conversion on two conditions: no demolition of residential buildings and a limited amount of new market-rate construction. After NYCHA and tenant leaders chose Related and Essence to lead the project, community meetings were held, and tenants were bused to sample properties to demonstrate the companies’ good work. In 2022, Keitt recalled, the developers promised that tenants would receive renovation plans the following year. Instead, tenants received a shock. In 2023, NYCHA and tenant leaders announced that it was now a demolition and redevelopment project. Many learned about the change from a press release, on social media, or from a story in The New York Times: “to improve public housing, new york city moves to tear it down.” Rebuilding was more cost-effective than renovating, officials explained. To rehab all 2,056 units would cost $1.14 billion, whereas the developers could reconstruct the buildings from scratch for just a touch more, at $1.3 billion. The main thing, though, was the benefit that the new plan would provide: Tenants’ apartments would be replaced with brand-new ones. Reconstruction would occur in phases, meaning that nearly everyone would move only once, directly into their new homes. The few tenants who were required to move twice would be placed temporarily into freshly renovated units on the same campus for the estimated three years that the first phase of construction would require. A rezoning would allow the developers, over at least the next 16 years, to deliver retail spaces and apartments to the housing-starved city, including 3,500 mixed-income units, with most renting at market rate and approximately 1,000 restricted to middle earners. A survey, administered by NYCHA, showed that tenants preferred this course of action. Much about this change of plans outraged tenants who had been part of the process. The renovation estimates used to justify wholesale demolition, which had ballooned from $492 million to more than $1 billion when rerun by the developers, seemed fishy to say the least. Tenants believed that their buildings were in sound structural condition. And NYCHA and its partners helped nothing by failing to provide a third-party building condition and cost report, claiming that it was not officially required by HUD now that the plan was to redevelop. In 2025, the figures were called into question by a former NYCHA chief architect, who balked at the notion that rehabilitation costs could have doubled in the space of two years and suggested that the numbers were likely invented to support the partners’ preferred plan. (NYCHA contends that it has provided tenants and community groups with cost estimates. New buildings will provide a higher “degree of preservation,” a spokesperson said, meaning that they will last longer before needing repairs, not to mention offer greater value for NYCHA and the city.) Meanwhile, the housing authority and the companies stood to split $16.3 million annually in revenue from the first Section 8 tower alone. Tenants, of course, wanted repairs for their homes. But they suspected that the land they lived on was becoming a piggy bank to cover NYCHA’s capital shortfalls and “unlock tremendous value,” as the project’s website put it, for two real estate giants. Particularly galling to skeptics was the claim that tenants themselves had chosen the new plan. The survey in question had asked them to pick between “rehabilitation of existing units” or two types of “new construction.” Nowhere was the term “demolition” used. Only 29 percent of the population of 3,388 eligible tenants responded; 57 percent, 550 tenants total, marked a preference for new construction. Now, NYCHA and the developers were trotting out these results to claim consent. “I’ve never seen anything so obviously disingenuous,” said Thompson, of the Community Service Society, who worked with tenants throughout the process. “It was just terribly, terribly dishonest.” An irony of all this engineering is that it only hardened some tenants’ opposition. Their resistance was not limited to objections about an illegitimate process. As details emerged, tenants learned of significant material costs inherent in the plan. For one thing, conversion to a Section 8 lease and private management would mean a loss of certain protections afforded them by conventional public housing—despite New York City’s expanded rights for program participants. Tenants, for example, are no longer permitted to transfer into other complexes. Most consequential is a seriously defanged grievance process for issues like nonpayment of rent and succession of tenancy after a relative moves or dies, legal advocates have said, with private landlords moving more quickly to remove tenants and frequently bypassing required procedures intended to keep them housed. “We know that there is an increased eviction rate after a conversion,” said Celines Miranda, a lifelong resident of Elliott-Chelsea and vice president of its resident association, who strongly opposes the plan. “This is an issue throughout the city as a whole.” In addition to threatening tenant rights, the redevelopment of Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea would gobble up valued open space, reducing well-used playgrounds and recreation areas across the two campuses by roughly 28 percent to make way for mixed-income buildings. In their place, developers have proposed an uninspiring set of new playgrounds and pocket parks that would largely be divided by massive high-rises or enclosed within their courtyards, disconnected from the sidewalk and the neighborhood. “If you look at the before-after renders, there is no significant improvement,” explained Matthias Altwicker, an architecture professor at the New York Institute of Technology who studies open space in NYCHA developments, and is otherwise a proponent of the city’s version of the RAD program. “These are terrible spaces compared to the existing through-block playground and sitting areas that were typical of NYCHA historically.” Meanwhile, tenants like Ruffin, who were expected to relocate during construction, would lose their neighbors as they moved to temporary apartments in buildings where they knew nobody. Even under the best circumstances, the strong networks of the complexes would be radically disrupted. “We will lose a sense of community, something that has been so essential in our lives,” Miranda said. In her professional life, Keitt had seen beloved community gardens destroyed when developers wished to erect towers on the land, with little regard for the harm it caused, she told me. Now, she looked at the plan for her home and recalled the botched public housing redevelopments of cities like Chicago. She glanced around her own city and saw NYCHA partnering with notorious slumlords like Pinnacle Group that subjected tenants to miserable conditions. Keitt decided to fight. At tenant meetings, she met Miranda and other neighbors who distrusted demolition. Together, they knocked on every door across the complexes, collecting more than 1,000 signatures on a petition against the plan, nearly double the number who selected “new construction” on NYCHA’s survey. Today, Keitt and Miranda not only are officers in their resident association but also lead the Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea Tenants Against Demolition, a multigenerational, multilingual group of residents that crashes NYCHA board meetings, testifies at City Council hearings, and stages rallies outside the Related Companies’ glassy Hudson Yards HQ. “It’s a constant fight, a constant battle every day,” Keitt said. “There’s a sense of violation of our homes. I’m worrying about the seniors. I’m worrying about everyone.” There are, of course, pro-demolition tenants who simply want improvements to their homes, come what may. Miguel Acevedo, the president of the Fulton Houses resident association, has been especially outspoken on behalf of those eager for new construction. His attitude is basically pragmatic. Washington is not coming to the rescue, Acevedo reasoned: “If you have no funding, you get nothing fixed. If you get some type of funding, at least you have the opportunity for capital improvements.” Fears about poor-quality redevelopment are unfounded, he told me. Related and Essence are “the best of the best.” Tenant opposition he dismissed outright as being ginned up “through lies.” His position has resulted in some pretty ugly confrontations in community meetings with the anti-demolition crowd. NYCHA and the real estate companies, for their part, are adamant that the project responds to tenants’ wishes. Engagement is their maxim. Jamar Adams, who spent his early years in public housing and played professional football before founding Essence, has become the face of the project. He points to an input process that entailed more than 65 community meetings. “I brought the transparency, the thoughtfulness, the desire to engage with the residents and not make decisions without them,” Adams told me. “I see a lot of the residents very much like I see my family.” Despite this familial thoughtfulness, however, many participants still ended up feeling blindsided—and pushed to the margins of their community. The Chelsea neighborhood, over the last two decades, has witnessed a dramatic influx of wealth in one of the most extreme gentrification processes in the country. Part of the rationale for allowing developers to clear public land for new housing is that it will absorb the renters who want to live there, a supply-side logic that has gained traction in recent years. Adams is fluent in this line of rhetoric. “Everyone knows that we need housing,” he said, yet “we allow the loud minority to slow down and stop and delay much-needed housing stock in the city of New York, and it’s not OK.” But those in public housing can’t help noticing that the new mixed-income towers will include few if any rentals that they, their families, or their friends can afford. Neighbors of Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea have become involved in the fight. In the area, there is no shortage of well-heeled townhouse owners, middle-income renters, and social activists who have taken up the cause. Many were genuinely appalled to learn that the redevelopment could mean living alongside a construction zone for decades. They were similarly appalled by the city’s treatment of public housing residents, said Layla Law-Gisiko, the local Democratic district leader, who has been one of the plan’s most steadfast critics. “It became very clear that this was a major concern across Chelsea, not only for public housing tenants but for neighbors, local businesses, and residents of surrounding developments,” Law-Gisiko said. “As the scale and duration of what was being proposed became clearer, people became increasingly alarmed.” These forces, the “loud minority” to whom Adams apparently refers, now rally alongside tenants, and pro-demolition partisans have seized on that support to discredit the opposition. There’s an impressive level of message discipline on this score. “There are some very loud, vocal groups, and we have to be honest that those are somewhat organized by outsiders,” Heather Beck, NYCHA’s chief real estate officer, told me. “I think outsiders have come in and stoked concern with residents that it’s a ‘land grab,’” Adams said. “That’s NIMBY,” Acevedo said. “That’s selfishness.” Seemingly galvanized by these provocations, this coalition of supporters has poured time and money into scrutinizing the Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea plan by researching public documents and posing challenges in the courts. A variety of legal filings exploits everything from land-use arguments to state public housing statutes to tenant law in an effort to halt demolition. In several cases, Ruffin is a named plaintiff. “She has been harassed and threatened,” one filing reads. NYCHA is firm that its conduct is about working with tenants to find a resolution. “It’s absolutely not harassment,” said Bova-Hiatt. “It’s engagement.” The legal approach, however, has created obstacles. Early this year, tenants won a temporary restraining order, bringing all the engagement to a grinding halt, at least for a time. If tenants seem needlessly intransigent about a plan designed to build them brand-new homes, it’s worth considering the program’s record. When people fret about privatization of public goods, a primary concern is the drift away from strong democratic oversight. Across the country, turning public housing over to real estate barons has come with abuses undeterred by public regulatory agreements and accountability procedures, including failed relocations, wrongful evictions, and wretched living conditions. Miami offers the most vivid warning in its conversion of Liberty Square, the subject of a chilling PBS documentary that Keitt has screened at the Hudson Guild Theater as political education for her tenants. In a rapidly gentrifying district of the city, the housing authority worked with a subsidiary of Related Companies on a $300 million redevelopment of the historically Black public housing complex. Input sessions were held; promises were made to avoid displacement. But before the new mixed-income complexes came online, the housing authority turned around and offered tenants the option to take vouchers for the private market in place of their right to return to reconstructed homes. In the end, only five of the more than 600 original families remained in the community. Complaints about mold, leaks, and cracks in the walls have continued in the replacement buildings. San Francisco, one of the first cities to convert the bulk of its government-run stock, attracted $800 million in capital improvements across the system. Yet tenant complaints increased drastically for issues like lack of heat and hot water, plumbing malfunctions, and nonworking appliances. Private management companies have reportedly been combative about fixing routine problems. New York City, with its newfound will to remake an expanse of noncommodified brick towers into productive assets, provides some of the most extensive data on the outcomes of RAD conversions. More than 44,000 units have been converted to private management under the program since 2016, and another 18,000 are marked for inclusion. In a survey published in 2024, the Community Service Society found that tenants of converted properties were more likely to report that their new landlords met their repair needs—as should be expected, given the large capital infusions to the developments. At the same time, however, tenants were more likely to describe issues like leaks, mold, and faulty heat and hot water as “serious” than those in conventional NYCHA public housing. New York City tenants have also suffered more than 10,000 code violations in converted developments since 2021, according to data from the independent local news outlet The City Reporter. In the worst cases, such neglect has allegedly led to catastrophes like a recent gas explosion at the Boston Secor Houses in the Bronx. To account for the stacks of violations at converted developments, NYCHA has cited analysis by a housing research group showing that such conditions are acute during the construction phase but decrease after renovations are complete. But the aggregated data hardly explains the many alarming tenant complaints about particular landlords years after their buildings have been renovated, as captured by the Community Service Society, nor the hundreds of incidents, identified by The City Reporter, in which NYCHA has been forced to hire vendors to perform emergency repairs that private managers ignored. Converted properties in New York City have also shown higher eviction rates. One problem is the loss of a rigorous grievance process under private landlords, according to attorneys from the New York Legal Assistance Group. Tenants technically retain the right to request a hearing to dispute rent increases after a loss of income, resolve nonpayment, or plead for succession of tenancy. But it is significantly more burdensome for them to do so, and whereas the housing authority is prevented from pursuing evictions during the grievance process, private landlords under the program are not. That change has undermined succession rights and led to a shift away from NYCHA’s long-standing efforts to avoid removing tenants. Indeed, in 2024, eviction rates in NYCHA properties under private management were nearly five times greater than in conventional public housing, according to a report from the New York City comptroller’s office. NYCHA took exception to claims of a weakened grievance process, saying that it handles income recertifications and holds grievance hearings with tenants in a timely manner—and that it takes pains to protect public housing succession rights. The housing authority also challenged the findings of the comptroller’s eviction report. “The fact remains that there have been very few evictions” under the program, a NYCHA spokesperson said. “The program upholds resident rights and protections and provides households with ongoing social services and financial assistance to resolve existing rental arrears.” The agency’s own data shows that in 2025, eviction rates in converted properties were well below the citywide rate and in line with those in conventional public housing. Advocates, however, have continued to worry about systemic problems observed in the comptroller’s report, like routine failures by private managers to provide struggling tenants a copy of the grievance procedures or offer repayment agreements, as required before filing an eviction. Recognizing these problems, some advocates and policymakers have fought for federal funding to preserve the existing public housing system. The cost of full repair may sound insurmountable: A recent report from the Council of Large Public Housing Authorities found that it would take roughly $170 billion over the next 10 years to address the system’s needs. But compared, for example, to the $28 billion per year in mortgage interest deductions for homeowners, itself a form of subsidized housing, the price tag sounds less daunting, said Korey Lundin, a senior attorney at the National Housing Law Center. “The federal government could choose to do something different,” Lundin said. “Congress could choose to adequately fund federal housing.” A bit of hope glimmered in August, when Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez reintroduced the Green New Deal for Public Housing Act, a bill that would fully address the long-standing capital backlog in federal homes, modernizing them to be sustainable and environmentally resilient. That wager, however, has been shot down in the past, and in recent years Congress has mostly continued to place its bets on the private sector. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, recently passed into law with bipartisan support, makes the RAD program permanent and lifts the national cap on conversions by 100,000 units. The law also includes provisions intended to better enforce tenant rights in converted properties in the future, as well as an annual mandate for HUD to study the impacts of the program on residents. All the while, President Donald Trump’s HUD is chopping away at funding even for supposedly stable Section 8 assistance and taking measures to make it easier for cities to demolish or dispose of public housing. In the face of capricious federal decision-making, more grassroots policy demands have arisen. Ramona Ferreyra, the founder of the New York–based public housing preservation group Save Section 9, promotes an array of state and local taxes that could provide sustaining revenue. “People kept asking, how are you going to fund public housing?” said Ferreyra, a NYCHA tenant. “Funding the repairs is the only way to stop privatization.” A state proposal would tax every transaction that Wall Street processes, and the group requests that it earmark for NYCHA 5 percent of the proceeds, which would provide $2 billion in annual operating funds. Ten percent of a local tax increase on millionaires could bring NYCHA some $400 million per year. To finance renovations, Keitt favors the use of a program called Comprehensive Modernization, which has been responsible for revitalizing several NYCHA complexes when residents negotiated funding as part of local rezoning efforts. In the end, what tenants like Ferreyra and Keitt demand is straightforward: the option to preserve public housing, without unasked-for private entanglements. “What I would like to see is democracy at work,” Keitt said. “Ask people what they want. Give them choices.” In New York City, democracy has proved to be a contested proposition. Some advocates were hopeful that Mamdani would step in the way of what they see as privatization. On the campaign trail, he quoted liberally from New Deal Mayor Fiorello La Guardia and promised to double capital spending on NYCHA. For some, then, it felt like a heel turn when Mamdani took office and committed to moving full speed ahead with the Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea redevelopment. In a video from February, Cea Weaver, an accomplished organizer whom Mamdani appointed to lead the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants, could be seen at a meeting with residents of the complexes saying, “We are interested in continuing to move forward the plans here.” The room erupted in protest. Later, the anti-demolition group sent a letter to the mayor, requesting a halt to the project and a meeting with him. To date, he has not replied. Before long, the Mamdani administration came out in full-throated support of the program. His housing plan, released in May, devotes significant funding to the local version of RAD and a related program called the Public Housing Preservation Trust, which would lease properties to a public-benefit corporation. Unable to gain an audience with the mayor himself, the opposition has taken its message to a range of public forums. In July, several dozen agitators showed up at NYCHA’s Annual Plan public hearing, held in an airy auditorium in Downtown Brooklyn. Many wore T-shirts that read PROTECT PUBLIC HOUSING. One by one, they testified against the inclusion of thousands of new conversions in Mamdani’s 2027 budget. “Our buildings are sound and strong,” said Samantha Ortiz, a Fulton resident. “We want rehabilitation, no privatization.” Miranda urged tenants not to sign new Section 8 leases. Even policymakers chimed in. Council member Chris Banks, chair of the Committee on Public Housing, has been a skeptic of the program and advocates that all tenants get to vote on whether their properties will be converted. At the hearing, he questioned the Mamdani administration’s commitment to NYCHA residents. After Banks spoke, as an official attempted to call the meeting to order, the crowd broke into shouts: “Save Section 9!” Officials looked dourly out from the stage. Weaver seems unconvinced by these eruptions. She has, in many ways, become the spokesperson for the mayor-as-landlord, in part because she’s unusually willing to respond to critics, scrapping with anti-privatization crusaders on X and absorbing the most searing accusations from tenants. (Section 8 is “a form of public housing,” Weaver told Keitt when they clashed at a recent NYCHA tenant forum hosted by the mayor’s office. “I’m not understanding how you keep telling my tenants that,” Keitt replied. “It’s not the truth.”) A onetime opponent of the RAD program, Weaver is now a true believer. Above all, she emphasizes its publicness. The program is a more “politically stable, hopeful option for a democratic socialist administration,” Weaver told me. NYCHA maintains control, with the private partner enjoying little more than a “vendor relationship” to the public agency. Strong accountability measures encouraged by the city—including a “roundtable” of providers to support tenants during conversion, and potentially even “co-management” agreements between resident associations and new private landlords—will help enforce tenant rights and monitor renovation quality. If landlords fail to uphold their end of the agreement, NYCHA can always kick them out. “Everything about this is made possible through public money, public control over the asset,” Weaver said of the program. “This is something that is entirely with the public sector in the driver’s seat, and that’s important because the public is where democracy happens.” What gets lost in policy debates is that the people who actually live in public housing may have separate motivations from those of political and real estate elites. For them, it doesn’t seem like NIMBYism to say that they don’t want their perfectly good apartment buildings razed for the sake of the bottom line. Anti-demolition tenants have a different form of democracy in mind, one in which they make the final decisions about the fate of their homes. That fate will far outlast the oversight intentions of the Mamdani administration. What gets lost in policy debates is that the people who actually live in public housing may have separate motivations from those of political and real estate elites. It doesn’t seem like NIMBYism for them to say that they don’t want their perfectly good apartment buildings razed for the sake of the bottom line. It doesn’t sound outrageous to ask the city, which funded public housing for decades, to scrounge up money to sustain it—at least as much as it finds for programs like police and schools. Nor does it seem strange to expect the new mayor, who promised to tame the excesses of the private sector, to protect working people rather than surrendering them to the whims of profiteers. In July, an appeals court lifted the temporary restraining order that had throttled the plan at Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea. For developers, that means it’s open season. Yet NYCHA must turn the buildings over unoccupied. The Mamdani administration, high priests of pristine optics, would prefer to avoid the spectacle of hauling seniors into housing court. At the moment, the city’s approach is “bespoke, one-on-one engagement,” according to NYCHA, with groups of city officials knocking on holdouts’ doors to inform them of their rights and persuade them to move into temporary apartments. As of late September, there were no takers. But in the end, the housing authority is a landlord, with all the tools of one. Recently, it delivered lease-termination notices to those who remain. The agency has repairs to consider, revenue, and especially development—not just of homes for the “ill-housed, ill-clad, ill-nourished” of the Roosevelt era, but these days, apparently, for all of Gotham’s twinkly-eyed in-movers. “We never want to evict somebody,” Bova-Hiatt said. “But we can’t let a handful of people stand in the way of progress.” Doris Ruffin has remained immovable. Early one Friday in August, Ruffin took her morning walk, four laps of the track at Chelsea Park, across from her building’s front door. On the soccer field, it was peaceful. Runners lapped the red clay track in the rising heat. Someone kicked a soccer ball around the damp grass of the field. The exercise and fresh air helps with her condition. “I’m not going anywhere,” she said, mustering the resolve of a cancer survivor at the prospect of NYCHA taking her to housing court. “I’m going to fight tooth and nail.” But all the uncertainty is stressful, she said. Will her home be demolished? Will it ever be rebuilt? Will her new landlord be worse than the last? She loses sleep. “I put in my time,” she said. “I worked. I should be able to live in peace, not worrying about who’s going to knock on my door.” She has contributed to her family and community, paid hundreds of thousands of dollars in rent to landlords in the private and public sectors. Now she’s sick. What she wants, she feels, is simple: repair without loss, improvement without displacement. For some reason, this city, this state, this country are no longer designed to provide that. Michael Friedrich is a journalist who writes about culture and cities.

It was another wild ride for Fantasy football managers in Week 7, with breakout performances, unexpected heroes, and some frustrating disappointments rewriting the landscape. We kicked things off with a shootout between two of the best young quarterback in the NFL. Drake Maye continued his incredible hot streak, putting together another monster performance, while Caleb Williams showcased his growing potential with back-to-back 300-yard passing games.  But Week 7 wasn't all good news, as several highly anticipated players failed to live up to expectations, leaving fantasy managers searching for answers heading into Week 8. Injuries, inconsistent usage and disappointing offensive performances once again played a major role in determining fantasy outcomes. Let's take a deeper dive into the Fantasy stockwatch after Week 7 heading into Week 8.  Pittsburgh 16 – New Orleans 10 Etienne is eligible to come off IR in Week 9 (the Saints have a bye in Week 8). This team cannot run the football and desperately needs Etienne to inject some life into the run game. I think he'll be a decent RB2 going forward (assuming he is back in Week 9). New York Giants 27 – Houston 21 Collins just had his second straight game with only five targets, and today he turned those targets into just 2.6 PPR Fantasy points. In Week 6, Collins was shadowed by Travis Hunter. This week, he was shadowed by Deonte Banks. That's no excuse! It wasn't the best day for C.J. Stroud (17-28/153/2), and I think I'd be buying low on Collins, but that's with the expectation of him being a WR2 for the rest of the season. Right now, I can't treat him like a WR1. Cam Skattebo led the way with 17/124/1 and one reception, but he split touches pretty evenly with Tyrone Tracy Jr. before Tracy left with an injury. After the injury, Devin Singletary factored in. My guess is that Skattebo will split with Tracy if Tracy is healthy after the bye week. Also, this was by far the best performance by the Giants' run game this season. I can't buy in fully. It's great that you can use Skattebo as an RB2 or maybe a flex going forward, but I wouldn't expect this to game to catapult him to must-start status. Since J.J. McCarthy took over in the fourth quarter of Week 6, Isaiah Likely has a 15.9% target share. You know who McCarthy is targeting a lot? Yes, Malik Nabers of course. But Malachi Fields has a 22.7% target share with McCarthy. Right now, it's coming at Likely's expense. Atlanta 29 - San Francisco 20 The 49ers have a bye in Week 8 and will hopefully be healthy for Week 9. I expect Purdy to get back on track once Mike Evans and/or Deebo Samuel are healthy. This is three straight games without a TD and with fewer than 18 PPR points. He had a three-game stretch (Weeks 8-10) last season that was even worse than this stretch, and then he dominated Fantasy Football for the rest of the season. Cincinnati 35 – Baltimore 13 Brown dominated snaps and touches, yet he came away with another disappointing game. I was concerned Samaje Perine would have a bigger role, so I'm relieved that didn't happen. However, Perine did have a goal-line TD run, and Brown once again was inefficient as a ball carrier. The only reason Brown is a must-start player right now is that running back sucks so bad. My gut tells me that once Lamar Jackson comes back, Henry will regain his form. But he is 32 years old, after all, and is now averaging 3.9 ypc this season. For the first time in his career, Henry has gone six straight games (within the same season) averaging 4.3 ypc or less. Tampa Bay 43 – Carolina 13 I'm willing to call it a bad day at the office. Start the four main Panthers next week against the Packers. Miami 28 – New York Jets 25 Only five targets for Cooper, but he caught all of them for 115 yards and a TD. I had my doubts about Cooper, and honestly, if you told me he was only going to get five targets, I would have confidently sat him. I think I have to recommend him as a starter next week against the Raiders. Is Cooper the new WR1 for the Jets? Nah! Garrett Wilson (three catches for 26 yards on three targets) will bounce back. This is Gordon's third straight game with 88 or more rushing yards and a TD. I would consider selling high on him (though I feel like I've said that too many times already) because he doesn't have much of a role in the passing game, and the Dolphins will be facing some great offenses in the coming weeks. That could lead to bad game scripts. Or, you could just keep him because he's a workhorse who is playing well. Cleveland 27 – Tennessee 24 The second three-TD game of Pollard's career! Unfortunately, he was started in only 49% of CBS leagues. I get it. This was Pollard's first game with more than 13.6 PPR FPs. He has dominated carries all season long but had just one TD entering the game. I think you have to look at him as a low-end RB2 going forward. I just don't think the Titans offense will create enough scoring chances for him. Also, Tyjae Spears was out today, which probably helped a little. I view Pollard similarly to Ollie Gordon. Finally, we get the breakout game for Concepcion, who had eight catches for 129 yards and nearly had a TD. I don't think this means he is a reliable starter, but he is a must-roster player who can be a flex for your Fantasy team. Minnesota 16 – Indianapolis 10 Bad performance in a great matchup. At least he rushed for 39 yards. That's actually quite encouraging, and his schedule is as good as it gets for the next few weeks (@DET, BUF, @GB). Don't give up on him yet, but you have every right to be disappointed with this performance! © 2026 CBS Interactive Inc.
